questions.question: Which cell type produces the myelin sheath? Options: A neurone, B rod cell, C Schwann cell, D lymphocyte.
questions.answer: C - Schwann cell
steps: Myelin is a fatty sheath that wraps around an axon and acts as an electrical insulator.
In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is made by Schwann cells, which wrap round the axon many times.
Neurones carry impulses but do not make myelin, rod cells are light receptors and lymphocytes are immune cells.
So the correct option is C, Schwann cell.

questions.question: Which row of a table correctly compares impulse conduction along a myelinated neurone with a non-myelinated neurone?
questions.answer: A: faster; because depolarisation only takes place at the nodes of Ranvier
steps: Myelin insulates the axon, so ion movement and depolarisation can occur only at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier).
The impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), so conduction is faster than in a non-myelinated neurone.
So the row is 'faster' and 'at nodes of Ranvier', which is A.

questions.question: Describe the role of ion transport in maintaining the resting potential of a neurone (4 marks).
questions.answer: The Na+/K+ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in; K+ leaks out more readily than Na+ leaks in, so the inside is negative.
steps: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP (active transport) to move 3 Na+ out of the axon for every 2 K+ moved in.
This keeps Na+ concentrated outside and K+ concentrated inside the axon.
The membrane is more permeable to K+ (K+ leak channels), so K+ diffuses out down its gradient more than Na+ diffuses in.
Loss of positive ions from inside leaves the inside negative relative to the outside, giving a resting potential of about -70 mV.

questions.question: Using the graph of the effect of TTX on the nerve impulse in an axon, deduce how TTX inhibits nerve impulses (3 marks).
questions.answer: TTX blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, so too little Na+ enters, the membrane does not depolarise to threshold and no action potential forms.
steps: In the untreated axon the membrane depolarises from -70 mV to about +50 mV, but in the TTX-treated axon it only reaches about -45 mV, never positive.
Depolarisation is caused by Na+ entering through voltage-gated sodium channels, so a much smaller rise means TTX has stopped most of these channels from opening.
Without full depolarisation the threshold is not passed, so no action potential is produced and the impulse cannot be conducted along the axon.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the phrase 'gene variants' (paragraph 4 of the source article) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Different forms of the same gene, with slightly different DNA base sequences, so they can code for slightly different proteins.
steps: A gene is a sequence of DNA bases that codes for a polypeptide.
Gene variants (alleles) are different versions of the same gene.
They differ in their base sequence, for example through substitution or deletion mutations.
This means they can produce versions of a protein with different structure or effects.

questions.question: Explain why tumours riddled with different mutations are good candidates for immunotherapy (4 marks).
questions.answer: Many mutations give many abnormal proteins (antigens) that the immune system recognises as non-self, so lymphocytes can be targeted to attack the tumour.
steps: Tumour cells with many mutations make many abnormal proteins on their surface.
These altered proteins act as antigens that the immune system recognises as non-self.
More different antigens give more targets, so more lymphocytes (T cells) can be activated against the tumour.
Immunotherapy boosts these lymphocytes, and a tumour with many targets is less likely to escape all of them.

questions.question: Explain why a CT scan was used to show that Judy Perkins was free of tumours (paragraph 10 and Figure 1) (2 marks).
questions.answer: A CT scan gives detailed cross-sectional images of the body's internal organs, so it can show deep tumours and show that none remain.
steps: Tumours in the liver, lungs or other organs cannot be seen from outside, and a CT scan uses X-rays to build 3D images of soft tissue deep inside the body without surgery.
Scans before and after treatment can be compared to show that the tumours have shrunk or disappeared, and the whole body can be checked for any new tumours.

questions.question: Explain why a checkpoint inhibitor was given with the lymphocytes in the immunotherapy (checkpoint proteins prevent activation of immune cells) (2 marks).
questions.answer: The checkpoint inhibitor blocks checkpoint proteins, so the lymphocytes stay activated and keep attacking the tumour cells.
steps: Checkpoint proteins normally switch off immune cells such as T lymphocytes, to prevent damage to the body.
Tumour cells can use checkpoints to avoid being attacked by the immune system.
A checkpoint inhibitor blocks these proteins, so the lymphocytes are not switched off.
The activated lymphocytes can keep destroying the tumour cells.

questions.question: Explain how a gene variant that produces a defective form of an enzyme reduces the effectiveness of clopidogrel (4 marks).
questions.answer: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that the enzyme converts to its active form; a defective enzyme makes less active drug, so it works less well.
steps: Clopidogrel is a prodrug: it is inactive until it is changed into its active form.
The change is catalysed by a specific liver enzyme (CYP2C19 in the real drug).
A gene variant produces a defective enzyme, with a changed active site, so the enzyme works less well.
Less active drug is formed, so fewer platelets are inhibited and the protective effect of the drug is reduced.

questions.question: Suggest why blood vessels are required for functioning spinal cord tissue produced from stem cells (paragraph 31) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Blood vessels supply oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration (ATP) and remove waste such as carbon dioxide.
steps: Neurones and other cells in the tissue need a continuous supply of oxygen and glucose.
Blood vessels (capillaries) deliver these substances to the cells.
Aerobic respiration in mitochondria releases the ATP needed to maintain membrane potentials and transmit impulses.
Blood vessels also remove carbon dioxide and other waste products from the tissue.

questions.question: Suggest how a brew of growth factors and other proteins can stimulate induced pluripotent stem cells to produce functioning tissue (paragraph 33) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Growth factors bind receptors on the stem cells and switch on genes that make the cells differentiate into specific cell types.
steps: Growth factors are signalling proteins that bind to specific receptors on the cell surface membrane.
This triggers a signal transduction pathway inside the cell.
The pathway activates transcription factors that switch on particular genes.
The genes expressed make the cells differentiate into the specialised cells, such as neurones and blood vessel cells, that the tissue needs.

questions.question: From the graph, estimate how long the MDMA concentration in the blood takes to become 0.0 g dm-3 (1 mark).
questions.answer: About 12 hours
steps: After its peak the MDMA concentration falls roughly linearly: 46 at 4 h, 36 at 6 h, 23 at 8 h, about 6 units per hour.
Extending this line to 0 gives 8 + 23/6 = about 12 h (accept 11 to 13 hours).

questions.question: Calculate the rate of removal of ADH from the blood between 4 and 8 hours, from the graph (2 marks).
questions.answer: About 0.33 pmol dm^-3 per hour (decrease)
steps: Read the ADH curve on the right-hand axis: about 2.8 pmol dm^-3 at 4 h and 1.5 pmol dm^-3 at 8 h.
Change = 2.8 - 1.5 = 1.3 pmol dm^-3 over 8 - 4 = 4 h.
Rate = 1.3 / 4 = 0.33 pmol dm^-3 h^-1 (accept 0.30 to 0.35).

questions.question: Comment on the role of ADH in MDMA-induced brain swelling, using the graph and the laboratory results table (6 marks).
questions.answer: MDMA raises ADH, which makes the kidneys reabsorb too much water, lowering blood sodium concentration, so water moves into brain cells by osmosis and the brain swells.
steps: Graph: ADH rises from 1.5 to about 4.0 pmol dm^-3 within 2 h as MDMA peaks (about 47 ug dm^-3), then falls back to 1.5 by 8 h as MDMA is removed, so MDMA stimulates ADH release.
Table: at 9 h ADH is 4.5 pmol dm^-3, three times the normal 1.5 value, whereas at 96 h it is back to 1.2 pmol dm^-3.

High ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so too much water is reabsorbed and the blood is diluted: sodium concentration is only 112 mmol dm^-3 at 9 h, against 131 at 96 h and a normal 135 to 145.

Thirst also leads to drinking a lot, adding to the dilution; the blood has a higher water potential than the brain cells, so water enters them by osmosis and the brain swells (CT swollen at 9 h, normal at 96 h).
Only one case is given, and a link is not proof of cause, but the changes in ADH, sodium and swelling all go together.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between light intensity and pupil diameter, using the table of results (2 marks).
questions.answer: Pupil diameter decreases as light intensity increases for both lights, and the decrease is greater for LED light.
steps: Incandescent light: diameter falls from 25.5 mm at 0 a.u. per m^2 to 16.0 mm at 1400 a.u. per m^2, a fall of 9.5 mm, with no change between 75 and 150.
LED light: diameter falls from 25.5 mm to 9.5 mm, a fall of 16.0 mm, and is smaller than incandescent at every intensity above zero (e.g. 12.0 against 17.5 mm at 650).

questions.question: Calculate the amount of incandescent light passing through the pupil at 1400 a.u. per m2, using pi = 3.14 (3 marks).
steps: At 1400 a.u. per m^2 the incandescent pupil diameter is 16.0 mm, so the radius is 8.0 mm = 0.0080 m.
Amount of light = intensity x area = 1400 x 2.01 x 10^-4 = 0.28 a.u.

questions.question: Describe how light entering the eye causes the pupil to respond (4 marks).
questions.answer: Photoreceptors detect the light, impulses travel along the optic nerve to the brain, and the iris muscles change the pupil diameter.
steps: Light enters the eye and is absorbed by photopigment in the rods and cones of the retina.
The photopigment changes shape, changing the receptor's membrane potential and reducing or increasing neurotransmitter release.
Impulses pass along the optic nerve to the brain, which runs the pupil reflex.
Parasympathetic impulses reach the iris, so circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, and the pupil constricts in bright light.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term pluripotent stem cell (2 marks).
questions.answer: A stem cell that can differentiate into almost any of the many cell types of the body.
steps: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and differentiate.
Pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into many different cell types.
They can form almost every cell type in the body, but not the extra-embryonic tissue such as the placenta.
So the definition is a stem cell that can differentiate into almost any cell type of the body.

questions.question: Suggest why the retinal epithelial layer is checked to ensure no stem cells are present before it is placed in the patient's eye (2 marks).
questions.answer: Remaining stem cells could keep dividing or differentiate into unwanted cell types, forming a tumour or unwanted growth.
steps: Stem cells divide by mitosis and can differentiate into other cell types.
Any undifferentiated stem cells left in the graft could keep dividing in the eye.
This could form a tumour or a mass of unwanted cell types.
So the check makes sure only the correct retinal epithelial cells are transplanted.

questions.question: Explain how the pupil size changes when moving from dim to very bright light (3 marks).
questions.answer: Circular iris muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so the pupil constricts and less light enters the eye.
steps: Very bright light is detected by photoreceptors in the retina.
Impulses are sent to the brain and then to the iris along parasympathetic neurones.
The circular muscles of the iris contract while the radial muscles relax.
The pupil diameter decreases, reducing the light entering the eye and protecting the retina.

questions.question: Describe the role of rhodopsin in causing changes in the polarisation of rod cells (4 marks).
questions.answer: Light makes retinal change shape within rhodopsin, which starts a cascade that closes sodium channels and hyperpolarises the rod cell.
steps: Rhodopsin is made of the protein opsin with retinal bound inside, in the rod cell membrane.
Light is absorbed by retinal, which changes from cis to trans form, changing the shape of rhodopsin.
This activates a G-protein cascade that closes sodium ion channels in the membrane.
Fewer Na+ ions enter, so the rod cell becomes hyperpolarised and releases less neurotransmitter.

questions.question: Comment on the effect of red and far-red light on germination of plantain seeds and the processes in their cells, using the table of results (6 marks).
questions.answer: Red light promotes germination and far-red light reverses it, because red light converts phytochrome Pr to active Pfr and far-red converts Pfr back to Pr.
steps: With only 1 s of far-red, germination is 92 to 100 % after every red exposure, so red light stimulates germination.
Increasing far-red exposure to 5 to 30 s sharply reduces germination (after 32 min red: 100 % to 20 % at 5 s and 4 % at 30 s), so far-red inhibits germination and cancels the red effect.
In the cells, phytochrome exists as Pr, which absorbs red light and changes to the active form Pfr; Pfr absorbs far-red and changes back to Pr, so the last light received sets the Pfr:Pr ratio.
Pfr switches on genes (for example for gibberellin and amylase production) that start germination, and low Pfr stops these genes being expressed.
Exposure matters: at 5 s far-red, germination was 20 % after 32 min of red but 67 % after 4 min, and at 960 s far-red only the 4 min group (92 %) recovered, which is anomalous.
Each result is a single value with no repeats or statistics, so the trends should be treated with caution.

questions.question: The body length of a leech decreases less each time it is touched. What is this effect called? A absorption, B adaptation, C habituation, D sensitivity (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - habituation
steps: The response becomes weaker with each repeated touch, although the stimulus is harmless.
A decreasing response to a repeated, non-harmful stimulus is called habituation.
Adaptation (B) describes structures adjusting to an environment over time, not a decreasing response.
Absorption and sensitivity do not describe a response that decreases with repeated stimuli.

questions.question: Why is it an advantage for the leech to respond in this way? A filters out important from unimportant stimuli, B reacts more quickly, C protects its habitat, D finds food more easily (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - it filters out what is important and what is not important to react to.
steps: Habituation means the animal stops reacting to repeated harmless stimuli.
This saves energy and time that would otherwise be spent on unimportant stimuli.
The animal can then respond to important stimuli, such as a real threat.
Options B, C and D describe speed, habitat and feeding, which habituation does not provide.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the fiddler crab predator experiment, using the two graphs (3 marks).
questions.answer: Female crabs run home less often as encounters increase (about 90 % to about 70 %), showing habituation, whereas males stay high (70 to 100 %) with no clear decline.
steps: Females: the percentage running home falls from about 90 % at the 1st encounter to about 70 % at the 20th, with fluctuations and a low of about 35 % at the 19th, so they become habituated to the repeated, harmless approach.
Males: the percentage stays between about 70 and 100 % throughout and shows no clear downward trend, so there is little or no habituation.
Males ran home more than females at almost every encounter (about 90 % average against 65 to 70 %), so the sexes respond differently to the predator, perhaps because of differing risk.

questions.question: Which statistical test would analyse the effect of the number of predator encounters on the percentage of crabs running home? A correlation coefficient, B Hardy-Weinberg, C index of diversity, D Student's t-test (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - correlation coefficient.
steps: Both variables (number of encounters and percentage running home) are numerical.
A correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of a relationship between two numerical variables.
Hardy-Weinberg tests genetic equilibrium and index of diversity measures species variety, so B and C are wrong.
A Student's t-test compares means between two groups, so D is not the best choice here.

questions.question: Explain why a myelinated axon conducts impulses faster than a non-myelinated axon of the same diameter (3 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse jumps between them (saltatory conduction).
steps: Myelin is an electrical insulator, so ions cannot flow across the membrane under the sheath.
Depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, the gaps in the myelin.
Local currents flow between nodes, so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).
Fewer depolarisations are needed along the axon, so the impulse travels faster than in a non-myelinated axon.

questions.question: Suggest how damage to myelin sheaths of neurones can lead to muscle weakness (2 marks).
questions.answer: Impulses are slowed or fail to reach the muscles, so fewer muscle fibres contract and the muscle is weaker.
steps: Damage to myelin stops saltatory conduction along the motor neurone.
Impulses travel more slowly, or ions leak so that the impulse is lost.
Fewer action potentials reach the neuromuscular junction, so less acetylcholine is released.
Fewer muscle fibres are stimulated to contract, so the muscle is weaker.

questions.question: Comment on the validity of a student's conclusion that myelin quantity is related to whether a person has dementia, using the table of results (2 marks).
questions.answer: The conclusion is partly valid: all three dementia groups have less myelin than the control, but the data cannot show cause, and sample sizes and other variables are not given.
steps: Supporting the conclusion: control 52 a.u. against 25 (vascular), 32 (Alzheimer's) and 42 (Lewy body), and the standard deviations do not overlap those of the control (e.g. 52 - 3.2 = 48.8 against 42 + 5.0 = 47), so the differences look real.

Limitations: a link does not prove that low myelin causes dementia (it could be a result), the sample sizes are not stated, and the amount differs between the dementia types, so 'dementia' as a whole is not a single cause; age, sex and the brain region sampled are not controlled, and no statistical test was done.

questions.question: Using the labelled heart diagram (P, Q, R), which statement correctly identifies the SAN, AVN and Purkinje fibres? (1 mark)
questions.answer: B: Q is the sinoatrial node (SAN) and P is the atrioventricular node (AVN)
steps: Q is in the wall of the right atrium near the vena cava, where the SAN (pacemaker) is found.
P is at the junction of the atria and ventricles, the position of the AVN, and R is at the base of the septum where the Purkinje fibres begin, so only B fits.

questions.question: Which term describes the cardiac impulse that starts without a nerve impulse? A diastole, B myogenic, C polarisation, D systole (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - myogenic.
steps: Cardiac muscle contracts without external nerve stimulation, with the impulse starting in the SAN.
This self-generated contraction is described as myogenic.
Diastole and systole are phases of the cardiac cycle (relaxation and contraction), not the origin of the impulse.
Polarisation describes the charge across a membrane, not the start of the heartbeat.

questions.question: Explain why the duration of the cardiac cycle changes during exercise (3 marks).
questions.answer: Exercise raises CO2 levels, chemoreceptors and adrenaline increase SAN firing, so heart rate rises and the cardiac cycle is shorter.
steps: During exercise muscles respire more, producing more CO2 and lowering blood pH.
Chemoreceptors detect this and send impulses to the medulla oblongata.
The medulla increases sympathetic impulses to the SAN, and adrenaline is also released.
The SAN fires more often, so heart rate increases and the duration of each cardiac cycle decreases.

questions.question: Calculate the stroke volume of the football player after training, using the table of cardiac output and resting heart rate (1 mark).
questions.answer: 88.2 cm^3 (per beat)
steps: Stroke volume = cardiac output / heart rate.
After training: 4500 cm^3 min^-1 / 51 beats min^-1 = 88.2 cm^3.

questions.question: Using the ECG trace in the diagram, calculate the footballer's heart rate (1 mark).
questions.answer: About 155 beats per minute (accept 150 to 160)
steps: Count the QRS spikes in the 7 s trace: 18 beats.
Heart rate = 18 x 60 / 7 = 154 bpm; equivalently the time between spikes is about 0.38 s, giving 60 / 0.38 = about 156 bpm.

questions.question: Comment on the changes in heart activity shown by two ECG traces recorded two hours apart (3 marks).
questions.answer: The heart rate has fallen from about 155 to about 69 beats per minute, so the cardiac cycle is much longer and the heart is returning towards its resting state.
steps: In the first ECG there are 18 beats in 7 s (about 155 bpm), with a gap of about 0.38 s between beats; the second shows 8 beats (spikes at about 0.8, 1.7, 2.6 s, etc.), a gap of about 0.87 s, so about 69 bpm.
The cardiac cycle has lengthened, especially diastole, so the P wave, QRS complex and T wave are well separated in the second trace but overlap in the first.
The beat spacing is regular in both, so the rhythm is steady; the rate is still above the resting 51 bpm, consistent with recovery after exercise as sympathetic stimulation and adrenaline fall.

questions.question: Name the chemical formed when light is absorbed by the photopigment in rod cells. A cis-retinal, B phytochrome, C rhodopsin, D trans-retinal (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - trans-retinal.
steps: Rhodopsin is the photopigment, made of opsin with cis-retinal bound to it.
Absorption of light changes cis-retinal into trans-retinal, which changes the shape of the molecule.
So trans-retinal is the chemical formed after light absorption.
Rhodopsin is the photopigment itself, not the product, so C is not the answer.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the effects of light absorption on cells in the retina?
questions.answer: B: rod cell hyperpolarised, bipolar neurone depolarised
steps: Light splits rhodopsin, which closes Na+ channels in the rod cell, so the cell becomes hyperpolarised.
The hyperpolarised rod releases less inhibitory neurotransmitter, so the bipolar neurone is no longer inhibited and becomes depolarised.

questions.question: Describe the effect of light intensity on the mean potential difference of bipolar neurones, using the table of results (2 marks).
questions.answer: Mean potential difference increases as light intensity increases, rapidly at first, then levels off at 20 mV from 12 a.u.
steps: It rises from 11 mV at 2 a.u. to 17 mV at 4 a.u. and 19 mV at 8 a.u., the steepest rise being at low intensities.
From 12 a.u. up to 20 a.u. the value stays at 20 mV, a plateau, so higher intensity gives no further change (maximum response).

questions.question: Calculate the percentage change in mean potential difference when light intensity increases from 4 to 12 a.u. (2 marks).
questions.answer: 17.6 % increase
steps: Potential difference at 4 a.u. = 17 mV and at 12 a.u. = 20 mV, so the change is 20 - 17 = 3 mV.
Percentage change = 3 / 17 x 100 = 17.6 % (17.65).

questions.question: Give two reasons why some people might object to the use of mammalian retinas in this investigation (2 marks).
questions.answer: Animals must be killed to obtain the retinas (animal welfare), and using animals for research raises ethical concerns.
steps: The retinas come from mammals that must be killed to obtain the tissue.
Many people object on animal welfare grounds, because the animals may suffer.
Others object on ethical grounds, because animals are used for research that does not benefit them directly.
Some people believe animals should not be used for research at all.

questions.question: Which statement describes the response of the iris muscles to increasing light intensity? A circular and radial muscles contract, B circular and radial muscles relax, C circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, D circular muscles relax and radial muscles contract (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax.
steps: Increasing light intensity causes the pupil to constrict.
Constriction needs the circular muscles to contract, reducing the pupil diameter.
At the same time the radial muscles relax.
Option D describes the opposite (dilation), so C is correct.

questions.question: From the oscilloscope trace, which is the resting potential of the axon? A -70 mV, B -78 mV, C 38 mV, D 108 mV (1 mark).
questions.answer: A: -70 mV
steps: The resting potential is the steady potential difference before the stimulus, and the trace before the spike sits at about -70 mV.
-78 mV is the undershoot after the spike and 38 mV is the peak, so only A is the resting potential.

questions.question: Which voltage-gated ion channels are open at point Y on the action potential trace? (1 mark)
questions.answer: C: voltage-gated potassium channels only
steps: Y is on the falling part of the trace, which is repolarisation.
Voltage-gated sodium channels have closed (inactivated) by then, while voltage-gated potassium channels are open so K+ flows out, so only C is correct.

questions.question: What is the state of polarisation of the membrane at point Z on the trace? A depolarised, B hyperpolarised, C hypopolarised, D unpolarised (1 mark).
questions.answer: B: hyperpolarised
steps: At Z the potential is slightly below the resting value of -70 mV (about -72 to -78 mV).
This overshoot happens because the K+ channels are slow to close, so the membrane is hyperpolarised before returning to resting.

questions.question: How many of three statements about action potentials are correct? Statements: magnitude proportional to stimulus strength; spread in both directions along the axon; refractory period after an action potential. A none, B one, C two, D three (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - two statements are correct.
steps: Action potentials are all-or-nothing, so their magnitude does not depend on stimulus strength; statement 1 is wrong.
Action potentials spread away from the point of stimulation in both directions along the axon; statement 2 is correct.
A refractory period follows each action potential, when a new one cannot be generated; statement 3 is correct.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Explain why maintaining a resting potential requires ATP (3 marks).
questions.answer: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move Na+ out and K+ in against their concentration gradients, maintaining the charge difference.
steps: The resting potential depends on unequal distribution of Na+ and K+ across the membrane.
Ions must move against their concentration gradients to keep this difference.
The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP (active transport) to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in.
Without ATP, ions would diffuse back down their gradients and the resting potential would be lost.

questions.question: Describe how a neurotransmitter transmits a nerve impulse across a synapse (4 marks).
questions.answer: Ca2+ enters the presynaptic knob, vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, and it binds receptors that open Na+ channels on the postsynaptic membrane.
steps: An action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob and depolarises its membrane.
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ diffuses into the knob.
Ca2+ causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release it into the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na+ channels so a new action potential is generated.

questions.question: Describe how L-DOPA reduces some symptoms of Parkinson's disease (3 marks).
questions.answer: L-DOPA crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine, replacing the lost neurotransmitter so motor neurones are stimulated again.
steps: Parkinson's disease results from loss of dopamine-producing neurones.
L-DOPA can cross the blood-brain barrier, but dopamine cannot.
In the brain L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by the enzyme decarboxylase.
Extra dopamine restores transmission across synapses, improving movement control and reducing symptoms.

questions.question: Explain how transcription factors are involved in the synthesis of dopamine (2 marks).
questions.answer: Transcription factors bind to DNA and switch on genes for the enzymes needed to make dopamine.
steps: Transcription factors are proteins that bind to specific sites on DNA near a gene.
This switches on transcription of the genes coding for enzymes in the dopamine pathway.
mRNA is made and translated into those enzymes.
The enzymes catalyse the steps that produce dopamine.

questions.question: Comment on the graphs showing the effect of the LRRK2 mutation on dendrites of dopamine neurones made from stem cells of three groups (3 marks).
questions.answer: Neurones from people with Parkinson's disease have fewer and shorter dendrites than controls, and LRRK2 neurones are similar to the unknown-cause group.
steps: Number of dendrites: about 6.0 per neurone in the control, against about 3.5 in both Parkinson's groups, and the error bars do not overlap the control.
Length: about 45 um in the control, against about 25 um (unknown cause) and 30 um (LRRK2), with no overlap between control and disease error bars.

LRRK2 and unknown-cause groups are similar in number and the error bars overlap on length, so the LRRK2 mutation does not seem to make dendrites any smaller than other causes; fewer, shorter dendrites mean fewer synapses and so reduced signalling.

questions.question: Complete the table with the name and function of each of three labelled brain regions (2 marks).
questions.answer: P (medulla oblongata): controls heart rate and breathing rate; Q: hypothalamus, regulates body temperature and water balance and controls the pituitary gland; R: cerebellum.
steps: P is the medulla oblongata, which controls involuntary activities such as heart rate, breathing rate and ventilation.
Q lies just above the pituitary in the centre of the brain, the hypothalamus, which regulates body temperature, osmoregulation and hormone release from the pituitary.
R is the cerebellum, already given as balance and coordinating movement.

questions.question: Which statement about CT scans is correct? A produced by absorbance of magnetic fields, B produced by absorbance of radio waves by deoxyhaemoglobin, C produces a cross-sectional image of a thin slice through the body, D studies brain activity while a person does tasks (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - a CT scan produces a cross-sectional image of a thin slice through the body.
steps: CT scans use X-rays passed through the body from many angles to build up an image.
The result is a cross-sectional image of a thin slice of the body.
Option A describes MRI and option B describes the MRI signal from deoxyhaemoglobin, not CT.
Option D describes functional imaging such as fMRI, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Describe how PET could be used to identify the part of the brain that is overactive during a seizure (3 marks).
questions.answer: A radioactive glucose tracer builds up most in the overactive, respiring region, and the emitted radiation shows where activity is highest.
steps: A radioactive tracer (for example a fluorine-18 labelled glucose) is injected into the blood.
Overactive neurones take up more glucose because they respire more.
The tracer emits positrons that annihilate with electrons to produce gamma rays, which the scanner detects.
A computer builds an image showing where the tracer is most concentrated, which marks the overactive region.

questions.question: Suggest how a seizure in one part of the brain could lead to an increase in body temperature (3 marks).
questions.answer: Overactive neurones and uncontrolled muscle contractions raise metabolic rate and heat production, and the hypothalamus may not control heat loss properly.
steps: During a seizure the overactive neurones use more ATP, so respiration increases.
Uncontrolled muscle contractions use more energy, and much of it is released as heat.
The extra respiration releases heat as a by-product, raising body temperature.
If the seizure affects the hypothalamus, the thermoregulatory control of heat loss may be disrupted, so temperature rises further.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle fibre (paragraph 2 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: A long multinucleate cell with a sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, many myofibrils made of actin and myosin, and sarcoplasmic reticulum storing calcium.
steps: A skeletal muscle fibre is a long, cylindrical, multinucleate cell formed by fusion of many cells.
It has a sarcolemma (cell membrane) enclosing sarcoplasm (cytoplasm) with many mitochondria.
Within the sarcoplasm are myofibrils, which contain repeating sarcomeres made of thick myosin and thin actin filaments.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum surrounds the myofibrils and stores Ca2+ needed for contraction.

questions.question: Explain how myokines may exert endocrine effects on organs such as the liver (paragraph 3 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Myokines are secreted by muscle into the blood, carried to the liver, bind receptors on liver cells and change liver metabolism or gene expression.
steps: Myokines are signalling proteins released by muscle fibres into the bloodstream.
Because they are carried in the blood, they reach distant organs such as the liver.
They bind to specific receptors on the membrane of liver cells, starting a signal transduction pathway.
This changes the activity of enzymes or gene expression in the liver, altering its metabolism.

questions.question: Explain why changes to muscle structure and composition in the elderly can affect their ability to rise from a chair (paragraph 4 of the source) (4 marks).
questions.answer: Muscle mass and fibre number fall and fast-twitch fibres decline, so less force can be generated to lift the body weight from a chair.
steps: With ageing, muscle mass decreases (sarcopenia) because muscle fibres shrink and are lost.
Fast-twitch fibres, which produce the most force quickly, decline in number more than slow-twitch fibres.
Less force can be generated by the quadriceps and other leg muscles.
The body weight cannot be lifted from the chair as easily, so rising becomes harder.

questions.question: Explain why Ca2+ binding to troponin C allows muscle fibres to contract (paragraph 5 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Ca2+ binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites, so myosin heads can bind actin and form cross-bridges that contract the muscle.
steps: Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated.
Ca2+ binds to troponin C, causing troponin to change shape.
This moves tropomyosin away from the binding sites on the actin filament.
Myosin heads can now bind actin to form cross-bridges, and ATP hydrolysis powers the power stroke that shortens the sarcomere.

questions.question: Explain how the high-energy phosphates provide the energy necessary for muscle activity (paragraph 11 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Hydrolysis of ATP (or phosphocreatine) to ADP and Pi releases energy used by myosin heads and by pumps in the muscle.
steps: ATP stores energy in its high-energy phosphate bonds.
Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy.
This energy is used to change the shape of the myosin head for the power stroke and to detach it from actin.
It also powers ion pumps such as the Ca2+ pump that restores the muscle to rest.

questions.question: Suggest explanations for the effects that a reduction in tendon stiffness from ageing could have on movement at a joint (paragraph 12 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Less stiff tendons transmit force less efficiently, so movement is slower and less powerful, and some force is lost as the tendon stretches.
steps: Tendons transmit the force from the contracting muscle to the bone.
A less stiff tendon stretches more before the bone moves, so force is lost as elastic deformation.
The joint therefore moves more slowly and with less power for the same muscle contraction.
Movement may also be less precise, since the tendon responds less quickly to changes in muscle force.

questions.question: Suggest how myostatin might act as a negative regulator of muscle growth (paragraph 13 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Myostatin binds receptors on muscle cells and starts a signalling pathway that switches off genes for muscle growth and protein synthesis.
steps: Myostatin is a signalling protein that binds to receptors on the surface of muscle cells.
This starts an intracellular signalling pathway, such as the SMAD pathway.
The pathway inhibits transcription of genes that promote muscle growth and protein synthesis.
Less muscle protein is made, so muscle growth is limited.

questions.question: Complete the table by filling in the names of each labelled part of the relay neurone diagram (2 marks).
questions.answer: L: dendron (or dendrite); M: dendrites; N: axon; O: synaptic knobs (axon terminals)
steps: L and M are the branching processes that carry impulses towards the cell body: L points to a stalk at the point where it splits into fine branches (dendron/dendrite) and M groups the dendrites.
N is the long axon leaving the cell body, which carries the impulse away.
O are the swellings at the ends of the axon branches, the synaptic knobs (terminals) where neurotransmitter is released.

questions.question: Lidocaine is used as a local anaesthetic. It works by: A blocking acetylcholine binding to its receptor, B blocking release of acetylcholine, C inhibiting potassium ion channels, D inhibiting sodium ion channels (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - inhibiting sodium ion channels.
steps: Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the neurone membrane.
With Na+ channels blocked, Na+ cannot enter and depolarisation cannot occur.
Action potentials are therefore not generated or conducted, so pain signals are not sent.
Options A and B concern the synapse and C concerns potassium channels, so D is correct.

questions.question: State the type of microscope used to produce the photograph of a nerve with an outer layer of connective tissue (1 mark).
questions.answer: Scanning electron microscope (SEM)
steps: The image shows the three-dimensional surface of the nerve with great depth of field and a magnification of x3300.
That is typical of a scanning electron microscope, not a light microscope or a transmission electron microscope, which gives a flat 2D section.

questions.question: Calculate the thickness of the connective tissue layer between points X and Y on the photograph, in micrometres (2 marks).
questions.answer: About 3.7 um (accept about 3.5 to 4.0 um)
steps: Measure the line X to Y on the photograph: about 12.3 mm.
Real size = image size / magnification = 12.3 mm / 3300 = 0.00373 mm.
Convert to micrometres: 0.00373 mm x 1000 = 3.7 um.

questions.question: Explain why a myelinated neurone conducts an impulse faster than a non-myelinated neurone of the same diameter (3 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), with fewer depolarisations needed, so conduction is faster.
steps: Myelin is an electrical insulator, so ion movement across the membrane under the sheath is prevented.
Depolarisation happens only at the nodes of Ranvier.
Local currents spread between nodes, so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).
Fewer depolarisations are needed along the axon, so the impulse travels faster than in a non-myelinated axon.

questions.question: In which structure are rod cells located? A iris, B pupil, C retina, D spinal cord (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - retina.
steps: Rod cells are photoreceptors that detect low light intensity.
Photoreceptors are located in the retina at the back of the eye.
The iris and pupil are parts of the front of the eye that control light entry.
The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system and does not contain photoreceptors, so C is correct.

questions.question: Describe the role of rhodopsin in rod cells (3 marks).
questions.answer: Rhodopsin absorbs light, and its retinal changes shape, which closes Na+ channels and hyperpolarises the rod cell, reducing neurotransmitter release.
steps: Rhodopsin is a photopigment made of opsin with retinal bound inside.
Light is absorbed by retinal, which changes shape (cis to trans), changing rhodopsin.
This triggers a cascade that closes sodium channels in the rod cell membrane.
The rod cell hyperpolarises and releases less neurotransmitter, changing the impulses sent in the optic nerve.

questions.question: Discuss how the results of the phototropism experiments (shown in the drawing of a coleoptile) support the role of a plant growth substance in the phototropic response (6 marks).
questions.answer: The results show the tip perceives light and makes a chemical that diffuses down the shoot and causes unequal growth, so bending towards light is controlled by a growth substance (auxin).
steps: Expt 1: the intact coleoptile bends towards light, but with the tip removed or covered by a black cap there is no bending, so the tip detects the light and is needed for the response.

Expt 2a: a plastic sheet that blocks the whole width below the tip stops the response, but one blocking only the lit side still allows bending, so a substance moves down from the tip on the shaded side.
Expt 2b: a gel layer, which lets chemicals diffuse through, does not stop bending, so the signal is a diffusible chemical rather than an electrical impulse.
Expt 3: a tip placed on one side of a cut stump in the dark makes it bend away from that side, so the tip produces a substance without light that stimulates cell elongation under it.
Together: auxin (IAA) is made in the tip and, with one-sided light, moves to the shaded side, so cells there elongate more and the shoot bends towards light.
These experiments show a chemical is involved but do not identify it, and the drawings show no replicates.

questions.question: Label the diagram of a section through the human brain to show the pituitary gland, medulla oblongata and cerebral hemisphere (3 marks).
questions.answer: Pituitary gland: the small rounded structure at the base of the brain, hanging below the centre front of the stalk; medulla oblongata: the lower part of the brain stem, narrowing as it joins the spinal cord; cerebral hemisphere: the large folded outer part of the brain.
steps: Draw a label line to the small oval gland attached under the centre of the brain, in front of the brainstem: pituitary gland.
Draw a label line to the lowest part of the brainstem, just above where it narrows into the spinal cord: medulla oblongata.
Draw a label line to the large wrinkled upper and outer region (not the cerebellum): cerebral hemisphere (cerebrum).

questions.question: Complete the table to show the parts of the brain and their functions (2 marks).
questions.answer: Cerebellum: balance and coordination of movement; medulla oblongata: control of heart rate; cerebral hemisphere: conscious thought, learning, memory and voluntary movement.
steps: Cerebellum: coordinates muscle movement, balance and posture.
Row 2 (control of heart rate): the part of the brain is the medulla oblongata.
Cerebral hemisphere (cerebrum): conscious thought, learning and memory, vision and hearing interpretation, and voluntary control of movement.

questions.question: Describe how the autonomic nervous system regulates the breathing rate when a person is resting (paragraph 1 of the source) (4 marks).
questions.answer: At rest the parasympathetic system dominates; the medulla receives chemoreceptor information and sends fewer impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so breathing is slow.
steps: The medulla oblongata in the brainstem controls breathing rate through the autonomic nervous system.
At rest, chemoreceptors detect normal blood carbon dioxide and pH.
The medulla sends impulses at a low rate via parasympathetic activity, so breathing stays slow.
The diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract less frequently, so each breath is shallow and the rate is low.

questions.question: Explain how neurones can respond to different neurotransmitter substances (paragraph 4 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Different neurotransmitters bind to different specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which open different ion channels or start different signalling pathways.
steps: Each neurotransmitter has a specific shape that fits a particular receptor protein.
Each receptor is linked to a particular ion channel or second messenger system.
Binding of the neurotransmitter to its receptor opens the linked channel, causing excitation or inhibition.
So the same neurone can respond differently depending on which neurotransmitter binds.

questions.question: Suggest how the activity of the sympathetic nervous system in immune organs could regulate inflammation (paragraph 7 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Sympathetic neurones release noradrenaline, which binds receptors on immune cells and reduces release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reducing inflammation.
steps: Sympathetic neurones in immune organs release noradrenaline (norepinephrine).
Noradrenaline binds to adrenergic receptors on immune cells such as macrophages.
This reduces the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Less inflammation occurs, so sympathetic activity can act to reduce inflammation.

questions.question: Explain how an electrocardiogram could be used to show that a person has postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) (Box 1) (2 marks).
questions.answer: An ECG records the heart rate: in POTS the ECG taken on standing shows a much shorter interval between beats (a sustained rise of at least about 30 beats per minute) than when lying down.
steps: Record an ECG while the patient lies flat, then again after standing, and measure the time between successive R waves (QRS complexes) to calculate heart rate.
In POTS the heart rate rises sharply and stays raised on standing (tachycardia, typically 30 bpm or more above the resting rate), with a normal rhythm and no other ECG abnormality.
Blood pressure does not fall to explain it, so the rate change is the diagnostic sign (the exact criteria are those given in Box 1).

questions.question: Explain how reflex circuits in the gut cause a bolus to move (paragraphs 10 and 11 of the source) (4 marks).
questions.answer: The bolus stretches the gut wall, stretch receptors send impulses through enteric neurones, and circular muscles contract behind while longitudinal muscles relax in front, pushing the bolus along.
steps: The bolus stretches the gut wall, activating stretch receptors.
Sensory neurones send impulses to enteric neurones (the local reflex circuit).
Motor neurones cause the circular muscles behind the bolus to contract, and the longitudinal muscles in front to relax.
This pushes the bolus forward along the gut (peristalsis).

questions.question: State what is meant by the term ischaemia (paragraph 12 of the source) (1 mark).
questions.answer: A restricted blood supply to a tissue, so the tissue receives less oxygen and glucose.
steps: Ischaemia is a reduction in the blood supply to a tissue or organ.
Less oxygen and glucose reach the cells.
Aerobic respiration in those cells is reduced.
Cells may be damaged if the blood supply is not restored.

questions.question: Suggest why embryological ENS cells may fail to colonise the bowel in a developing embryo (paragraph 13 of the source) (1 mark).
questions.answer: The cells may fail to migrate because of a gene mutation or a lack of the signals and receptors needed to guide them along the gut.
steps: ENS precursor cells migrate from the neural crest along the developing gut.
Migration depends on chemical signals and receptors that guide the cells.
A mutation in genes controlling migration, or a lack of these signals, can stop the cells reaching the bowel.
So the cells may fail to colonise the bowel.

questions.question: Explain how the interaction of microbial and other factors could result in gastrointestinal inflammation such as IBD (Box 2) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Genetic susceptibility and environmental factors such as diet or antibiotics change the gut microbiota and damage the gut barrier, so microbes and their products trigger an excessive, persistent immune response that causes inflammation.
steps: Factors such as genes, diet, antibiotics and stress disrupt the normal balance of gut microbes (dysbiosis) and weaken the epithelial barrier.
Bacteria and their products cross the damaged lining and are detected by immune cells, which release inflammatory cytokines and recruit more immune cells.
If the immune response is not switched off (and enteric neurone signalling also alters), the inflammation becomes chronic and causes tissue damage, as in IBD.

questions.question: Which term describes the space between a sensory neurone and a relay neurone? A axon, B cell body, C postsynaptic membrane, D synaptic cleft (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - synaptic cleft.
steps: The space between two neurones at a synapse is called the synaptic cleft.
The axon is part of the neurone itself, not the space between neurones.
The cell body is the part of the neurone containing the nucleus.
The postsynaptic membrane is the membrane on the far side of the cleft, not the space itself.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the function of a sensory neurone and a motor neurone (3 marks).
questions.answer: Both carry impulses along axons; sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, while motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.
steps: Both types of neurone transmit electrical impulses (action potentials) along their axons.
Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors towards the CNS.
Motor neurones carry impulses away from the CNS to effectors such as muscles or glands.
Sensory neurones have a cell body in a dorsal root ganglion and motor neurones have their cell body in the CNS, which is a structural contrast.

questions.question: Suggest why a person with Guillain-Barre syndrome has the symptoms of this disorder, where the immune system damages the myelin sheath of neurones (3 marks).
questions.answer: Damage to myelin slows or stops impulse conduction in sensory and motor neurones, so sensation, movement control and reflexes are lost.
steps: Myelin damage removes saltatory conduction, so impulses are slowed or fail to be transmitted.
Sensory impulses from the limbs cannot reach the brain, so sensation is lost.
Motor impulses cannot reach the muscles efficiently, so steadiness when walking is lost.
Reflex arcs cannot transmit impulses quickly enough, so reflexes such as the knee jerk are lost.

questions.question: Explain how mutations in genes coding for voltage-gated calcium ion channels might cause neurological conditions (4 marks).
questions.answer: Mutated Ca2+ channels may not open or may let too much or too little Ca2+ enter the presynaptic knob, so neurotransmitter release at synapses is abnormal.
steps: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open when the action potential reaches the presynaptic knob.
Ca2+ entry triggers vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter.
A mutation can change the channel so it opens less or more than normal, or fails to close.
Abnormal Ca2+ entry changes neurotransmitter release, disrupting synaptic transmission and causing the condition.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the action of the two forms of phytochrome, Pr (P660) and Pfr (P730)? (1 mark)
questions.answer: A: Pfr absorbs far-red light and Pfr breaks down in the dark
steps: Pfr (P730) is the form that absorbs far-red light, which converts it to Pr.
Pfr is the unstable form and breaks down or reverts in the dark, while Pr is stable, so A is correct.

questions.question: Explain the role of auxins in the phototropic response of a shoot, using the diagram of auxin molecules (3 marks).
questions.answer: Light from one side makes auxin move to the shaded side, where it stimulates greater cell elongation, so the shoot bends towards the light.
steps: With light from directly above (first shoot) auxin is evenly spread on both sides, so both sides elongate equally and the shoot grows straight.
With light from one side (second shoot) more auxin molecules are on the shaded side than on the lit side.
The higher auxin concentration on the shaded side makes cells there elongate faster (by loosening the cell walls), so the shoot bends towards the light, as in the third shoot (positive phototropism).

questions.question: Explain how gibberellins regulate starch hydrolysis in a seed, so that the starch can supply energy when the seed germinates (4 marks).
questions.answer: Gibberellin switches on genes for alpha-amylase by removing DELLA repressors, and amylase hydrolyses starch to sugars for respiration.
steps: Gibberellin binds to its receptor in the aleurone layer cells of the seed.
This causes DELLA repressor proteins to be broken down.
Transcription factors are then free to switch on genes for alpha-amylase, which is made and secreted.
Amylase hydrolyses starch into maltose and glucose, which are used in respiration for growth.

questions.question: Comment on the effect of IAA and the synthetic auxin NAA on the growth of Chlorella, using the graphs of different concentrations (4 marks).
questions.answer: Both IAA and NAA increased Chlorella growth compared with the control; IAA was most effective at 0.1 umol dm^-3 and the effect fell at higher concentrations, whereas NAA was most effective at 1 umol dm^-3, and IAA had the larger effect.
steps: IAA: all concentrations gave more cells than the control (21 x 10^6 cm^-3 at 72 h), with 0.1 umol dm^-3 the highest (about 33.5), then 1 (28.8) and 10 umol dm^-3 (24.2): the lower the concentration, the greater the growth.
NAA: all concentrations also rose above the control, but by less: 1 umol dm^-3 was best (about 25.8 at 72 h), 10 gave 23.0 and 0.1 gave 22.0, barely above the control (21.4).
Growth increased with time under all treatments; the best IAA treatment (about +12 x 10^6 over control at 72 h) is much more effective than the best NAA (about +4 x 10^6).
The natural auxin IAA is therefore more effective than the synthetic NAA, and the best concentration is different for each; only three time points and no repeats are shown.

questions.question: How many of three statements about habituation are correct? Statements: habituation is an anatomical adaptation; habituation is only observed in mammals; habituation only occurs after repeated exposure to the same stimulus. A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3 (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - one statement is correct.
steps: Habituation is a behavioural change, not an anatomical adaptation, so statement 1 is wrong.
Habituation occurs in many animals, not only mammals, so statement 2 is wrong.
Habituation develops only after repeated exposure to the same harmless stimulus, so statement 3 is correct.
One statement is correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Which row of the table is correct about a beluga whale responding to a stimulus using a spinal reflex arc? (1 mark)
questions.answer: B: relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord; cell body of the sensory neurone in the middle of the axon
steps: Relay neurones lie within the grey matter of the spinal cord, where cell bodies are found, while white matter contains myelinated axons.
The cell body of a sensory neurone is in the dorsal root ganglion, off to the side in the middle of the axon (not at its end), so only B is correct.

questions.question: Comment on the changes in heart rate of the whale when diving, using the graph of heart rate against dive duration (3 marks).
questions.answer: During a dive the heart rate falls to low values (about 2 to 9 bpm), and it falls further the longer the dive, but after surfacing it rises to a maximum (about 28 to 35 bpm) that is higher after longer dives.
steps: During a dive the maximum rate falls from about 9 bpm to about 6.5 bpm, and the minimum falls from about 6.5 bpm to about 2 bpm as dive duration goes from 0 to 16 minutes, so heart rate is much lower than at the surface (bradycardia).
This reduces oxygen use and conserves the oxygen stores, so longer dives need a lower rate.
The maximum rate at the surface rises from about 28 to about 35 bpm as the dive lengthens, to restore oxygen and remove CO2 and lactate, so the effort needed is greater after a longer dive.

questions.question: Explain how changes in heart rate are controlled when the whale returns to the surface immediately after a dive (3 marks).
questions.answer: On surfacing, chemoreceptors detect low oxygen and high CO2, the medulla increases sympathetic impulses to the SAN, and adrenaline raises heart rate.
steps: On surfacing, chemoreceptors detect low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in the blood.
These impulses are sent to the medulla oblongata in the brainstem.
The medulla increases sympathetic impulses to the SAN, and adrenaline is released from the adrenal glands.
The SAN fires faster, so the heart rate rises quickly to supply oxygen to the tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following produces ADH? A adrenal gland, B hypothalamus, C medulla oblongata, D pituitary gland (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - hypothalamus (ADH is made in the hypothalamus and stored/released by the posterior pituitary).
steps: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is synthesised by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus.
It travels along axons to the posterior pituitary, where it is stored.
The pituitary gland releases ADH into the blood but does not produce it.
So the best answer for 'produces' is B, the hypothalamus.

questions.question: Which structures does ADH act on? A capillaries, B collecting ducts, C proximal tubules, D ureters (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - collecting ducts.
steps: ADH is carried in the blood to the kidney.
It binds to receptors on cells of the collecting ducts.
This increases the insertion of aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed.
Capillaries, proximal tubules and ureters are not the target of ADH.

questions.question: Control of plasma concentration and blood volume is an example of which type of process? A countercurrent multiplier, B habituation, C negative feedback, D positive feedback (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - negative feedback.
steps: A change in plasma concentration is detected and corrected by the body.
The response reduces the original change, so it is negative feedback.
Positive feedback increases a change, so D is wrong.
Countercurrent multiplier and habituation are not homeostatic control of plasma concentration.

questions.question: Name the type of receptor in the body that detects changes in the plasma concentration (1 mark).
questions.answer: Osmoreceptors (in the hypothalamus).
steps: Changes in plasma concentration change the water potential of the blood.
Osmoreceptors are specialised receptors that detect these changes in water potential.
They are located in the hypothalamus of the brain.
When they detect a change, they signal the release or inhibition of ADH.

questions.question: Comment on the effect of the gibberellin on the growth of cereal plants, using the table of mean internode lengths (2 marks).
questions.answer: The gibberellin increases internode length above 10 ppm, most in the first internode (36 to 56 cm) and little in the second and third.
steps: At 0 and 10 ppm there is no effect on any internode (36, 19 and 14 cm).

Above 10 ppm the first internode lengthens with concentration: 36, 41, 52 and 56 cm at 0, 100, 1000 and 2500 ppm, a rise of about 56 %, whereas the second rises by only 3 cm (19 to 22) and the third by 1 cm (14 to 15).

questions.question: Suggest how the gibberellin causes the effect on the internode lengths of cereal plants (3 marks).
questions.answer: Gibberellin binds its receptor, DELLA repressors are broken down, and genes for cell growth are expressed, so cells in the internodes elongate.
steps: Gibberellin binds to its receptor (GID1) in the cells of the internode.
This leads to breakdown of DELLA repressor proteins.
Transcription factors are then free to switch on genes involved in cell elongation and division.
More cell growth in the internodes makes them longer.

questions.question: Which substance can transmit a nerve impulse from one neurone to the next? A acetylcholine, B ADP, C cholesterol, D NADP (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - acetylcholine.
steps: Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter released from presynaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft.
It binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane and triggers a new impulse.
ADP and NADP are coenzyme/energy molecules and cholesterol is a lipid, none of which transmit impulses.
So the answer is A, acetylcholine.

questions.question: Explain why the membrane potential changes between points 1 and 2 on the diagram of an action potential in a motor neurone (2 marks).
questions.answer: A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (-55 mV), so voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ floods into the axon, making the inside positive (+30 mV).
steps: The stimulus raises the membrane potential from the resting -70 mV to the threshold of -55 mV, which opens voltage-gated Na+ channels.

Na+ ions then diffuse into the axon down their electrochemical gradient, and the entry of more Na+ opens further channels (positive feedback), so the potential rises quickly from -70 mV to about +30 mV (depolarisation).

questions.question: Calculate the percentage difference in the gradient of the myelinated and non-myelinated neurones; the non-myelinated gradient is 0.5 (3 marks).
steps: The myelinated line passes through the origin and (20, 120), so its gradient m = 120 / 20 = 6.0 m s^-1 per um.
Non-myelinated gradient is 0.5 (given).
Percentage difference = (6.0 - 0.5) / 0.5 x 100 = 1100 %, taking the non-myelinated value as the reference (the myelinated gradient is 12 times as steep).

questions.question: Explain why the speed of conduction differs between myelinated and non-myelinated neurones (3 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), whereas non-myelinated axons conduct continuously and more slowly.
steps: Myelin is an electrical insulator, so there is no ion movement under the sheath.
Depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier.
The impulse therefore jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is faster.
A non-myelinated axon depolarises along its whole length, so conduction is slower.

questions.question: Explain how PET can be used to identify the change in activity in the brain after taking cocaine, comparing with a control scan (4 marks).
questions.answer: A radioactive tracer shows where glucose uptake and respiration are highest, so comparing the control and cocaine scans shows which brain regions became more or less active.
steps: A radioactive tracer, such as glucose labelled with fluorine-18, is injected before each scan.
Active neurones take up more tracer because they respire more.
The emitted positrons produce gamma rays that the scanner detects, showing where the tracer is concentrated.
Comparing the control scan with the scan after cocaine shows regions where activity has increased or decreased.

questions.question: Lesion A is spherical with a diameter of 1.97 cm. Calculate its volume, giving the answer to 2 decimal places (2 marks).
questions.answer: 4.00 cm3 (V = 4/3 x pi x r^3 with r = 0.985 cm).
steps: The radius is half the diameter: r = 1.97 / 2 = 0.985 cm.
Use the volume of a sphere: V = 4/3 x pi x r^3.
V = 4.18879 x 0.95567 = 4.0031 cm3, which is 4.00 cm3 to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: Calculate the actual width of lesion B between points X and Y on the MRI scan, to 2 significant figures (2 marks).
questions.answer: About 0.90 cm
steps: There is no scale bar, so use lesion A as the scale: S to T measures about 54 mm on the page and is 1.97 cm in life.
X to Y measures about 25 mm on the page, so the ratio is 24.7 / 54.2 = 0.456.
Actual width = 1.97 x 0.456 = 0.90 cm (2 s.f.).

questions.question: Suggest why a dye might be given during an MRI scan used to diagnose a brain tumour (1 mark).
questions.answer: The dye (contrast agent) makes tumour tissue and blood vessels show up more clearly against the surrounding tissue.
steps: MRI distinguishes tissues by differences in the signal from water and fat protons.
Tumours and surrounding tissue can look similar on an ordinary scan.
A contrast agent (dye) changes the signal and accumulates in tumour tissue or blood vessels.
This increases the contrast, so the tumour is easier to identify and locate.

questions.question: Explain why ADEM causes problems with walking, given that myelin is destroyed and lesions form in the brain (2 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin destruction slows or blocks impulses along motor neurones and within the brain's coordination centres, so movements of the legs are poorly coordinated.
steps: ADEM destroys myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord.
Without myelin, impulses along motor neurones are slowed or lost.
Lesions in the brain disrupt the coordination of movement, such as balance and timing of leg movements.
So signals to the leg muscles are poorly coordinated, causing difficulty walking.

questions.question: Which row in the table shows the effect of an increase in adrenaline in a mammal? (1 mark)
questions.answer: C: breathing rate increases and heart rate increases
steps: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight, so it increases both heart rate and breathing rate.
Only row C has both as increases.

questions.question: Deduce the effect of the combination of nicotine and adrenaline on the mean heart rate of Daphnia, using the table of results (3 marks).
questions.answer: Nicotine lowers the heart rate, and high-concentration adrenaline partly cancels this effect, but low adrenaline has almost no effect on the nicotine-treated hearts.
steps: Nicotine alone lowers the heart rate below the 146 bpm control at every concentration, and the higher the nicotine, the lower the rate (106 bpm at 0.001 down to 84 bpm at 1000 mmol dm^-3).
With the low adrenaline (0.001 mmol dm^-3) the rates are within about 3 bpm of those with nicotine alone (e.g. 105 against 103 at 0.1), so it hardly changes the nicotine effect.

With high adrenaline (0.1 mmol dm^-3) the rate is higher than with nicotine alone at every concentration (e.g. 104 against 84 at 1000, 151 against 106 at 0.001), so adrenaline acts against nicotine, and with the least nicotine the rate (151) is above the control.

questions.question: Which is a description of a gibberellin? A an enzyme that converts starch to glucose, B a molecule that converts Pfr to Pr, C an organic compound that stimulates the action of transcription factors, D a protein that wraps around DNA (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - an organic compound that stimulates the action of transcription factors.
steps: Gibberellins are organic plant growth substances (hormones) that act on genes.
They bind receptors and cause DELLA repressors to break down, freeing transcription factors to act.
Option A describes amylase, B describes an enzyme-like process of phytochrome, and D describes histones.
So the correct answer is C.

questions.question: Discuss how phytochromes and gibberellins affect flowering in plants, using the flashes of red and far-red light investigation and the graph of gibberellin concentration (6 marks).
questions.answer: Phytochrome changes with red/far-red light, so night length controls flowering: short-day plants flower only with a long uninterrupted night and long-day plants with a short or interrupted night; gibberellins, made when phytochrome signals are right, promote flowering up to an optimum concentration.
steps: Short-day plants flower when the dark period is above the critical night length (about 12 h), but not when the night is interrupted by red light; far-red straight after the red flash cancels it, so the last flash decides the result (red, then far-red, then red = no flowering).
Long-day plants do the opposite: they flower when the night is short or interrupted by red light and not when far-red is last.

Red light changes phytochrome Pr to active Pfr and far-red changes it back; in a long night Pfr falls (it breaks down in the dark), so the Pfr to Pr ratio signals night length and controls whether flowering genes are switched on.
Gibberellins are produced in response and switch on flowering genes (by breaking down DELLA repressors).

In the graph, the mean number of flowers rises from 1.0 at 0.3 umol dm^-3 to a maximum of 3.8 at about 1.5 umol dm^-3, then falls to 3.0 and 1.6 at 3.0 and 4.4, so there is an optimum concentration and high concentrations reduce flowering.

questions.question: Describe how the pupil of an eye dilates and contracts in response to changes in light intensity (4 marks).
questions.answer: In bright light circular muscles contract and the pupil constricts; in dim light radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax, so the pupil dilates.
steps: Photoreceptors detect the change in light intensity and send impulses to the brain.
In bright light parasympathetic impulses make the circular muscles of the iris contract, and the pupil constricts.
In dim light sympathetic impulses make the radial muscles contract while the circular muscles relax, so the pupil dilates.
Constriction limits the light entering the eye and dilation allows more light in, protecting the retina and improving vision in dim light.

questions.question: Which pair of molecules forms the photoreceptor in an eye? A auxin and retinol, B lysozyme and ribose, C opsin and retinal, D phytochrome and opsin (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - opsin and retinal.
steps: The photoreceptor in the eye is rhodopsin, a protein (opsin) with a light-absorbing molecule (retinal) bound to it.
Auxin and retinol are not photoreceptors, and lysozyme and ribose are not involved in light detection.
Phytochrome is a plant photoreceptor, not an animal one, so D is wrong.
So the correct pair is C, opsin and retinal.

questions.question: Which of these drugs would increase nerve transmission? A ecstasy (MDMA) and lidocaine, B ecstasy (MDMA) and nicotine, C lidocaine and nicotine, D lidocaine only (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - ecstasy (MDMA) and nicotine.
steps: Ecstasy (MDMA) increases the release of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and dopamine, increasing transmission.
Nicotine mimics acetylcholine and binds its receptors, so it increases transmission.
Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, which decreases transmission.
So the pair that increases nerve transmission is ecstasy and nicotine, option B.

questions.question: In direct sunlight the pupil diameter is 4 mm; in complete darkness the pupil area is 38.75 mm2. Calculate the increase in diameter (2 marks).
questions.answer: 3.02 mm (darkness diameter about 7.02 mm, minus 4 mm).
steps: r = sqrt(12.334) = 3.512 mm, so the diameter in darkness = 2 x 3.512 = 7.02 mm.
The diameter in direct sunlight is 4 mm.
Increase in diameter = 7.02 - 4 = 3.02 mm.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in mean pupil diameter when a person moves from bright light into darkness, using the table of mean pupil diameters (1 mark).
steps: Increase in diameter = 6.41 - 3.35 = 3.06 mm.
Percentage increase = 3.06 / 3.35 x 100 = 91.3 %.

questions.question: Which is the name of the hormone involved in the fight or flight response? A adrenaline, B antidiuretic hormone, C thromboplastin, D uracil (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - adrenaline.
steps: The fight or flight response is triggered by the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline.
Adrenaline is released from the adrenal medulla into the blood.
Antidiuretic hormone controls water reabsorption, not the fight or flight response.
Thromboplastin is involved in blood clotting and uracil is a base in RNA, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Describe how the increase in pupil diameter during fight or flight is brought about by the muscles of the iris (3 marks).
questions.answer: Radial muscles of the iris contract and circular muscles relax, so the pupil dilates.
steps: Sympathetic nerve impulses are sent to the iris during fight or flight.
The radial muscles of the iris contract, pulling the edge of the pupil outward.
The circular muscles relax, so they no longer narrow the pupil.
The pupil diameter increases, letting more light into the eye.

questions.question: Which type of scan can be used to study changes in brain function as they happen? A computed tomography (CT), B electrocardiogram (ECG), C functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), D polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
steps: fMRI detects changes in blood oxygenation linked to neural activity, so it shows brain function in near real time.
CT scans give structural images, not changes in function as they happen.
An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, not the brain.
PCR is a technique for amplifying DNA, so it is not an imaging technique.

questions.question: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of using PET and MRI to investigate brain function (3 marks).
questions.answer: PET uses a radioactive tracer that shows metabolic activity but exposes the patient to radiation and is expensive; MRI uses no radiation and gives detailed images but is costly and cannot be used with metal implants.
steps: PET shows changes in metabolic activity by detecting a radioactive tracer, which is a clear advantage for brain function.
The drawback of PET is that the patient is exposed to radiation and the tracer must be made in a cyclotron.
MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, so it avoids radiation and gives detailed structural images.
The drawbacks of MRI are that it is expensive, takes time, and cannot be used with patients who have metal implants.

questions.question: Complete the table to show one function for each labelled part of the section through the human brain (3 marks).
questions.answer: Cerebellum: coordinates movement and balance; cerebral hemisphere: conscious thought, memory, learning and voluntary movement; hypothalamus: regulates body temperature and water balance and controls the pituitary gland.
steps: Cerebellum: balance, posture and coordination of voluntary movement.
Cerebral hemisphere (cerebrum): conscious thought, learning, memory and the origin of voluntary actions.
Hypothalamus: homeostasis such as temperature and water potential (osmoregulation), and control of hormone release from the pituitary gland.

questions.question: Which description of ion movement will produce an action potential in an axon? A K+ ions move into the axon, B K+ ions move out of the axon, C Na+ ions move into the axon, D Na+ ions move out of the axon (1 mark).
questions.answer: C - Na+ ions move into the axon.
steps: An action potential begins when voltage-gated Na+ channels open.
Na+ ions diffuse into the axon down their electrochemical gradient, depolarising the membrane.
K+ movement out of the axon occurs during repolarisation, not to start the action potential.
So the correct answer is C.

questions.question: Which row describes the events that occur during repolarisation of a neurone? (1 mark) (table of rows not in text)
questions.answer: A: sodium ion channels closed, membrane potential decreasing
steps: During repolarisation the voltage-gated sodium channels have closed and voltage-gated potassium channels are open, so K+ leaves the axon.
The potential falls from about +30 mV back towards -70 mV, so it is decreasing; this is row A.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a spinal reflex arc (3 marks).
questions.answer: Receptor, sensory neurone to the spinal cord, relay neurone in the grey matter, motor neurone to the effector (muscle or gland).
steps: A receptor in the skin or organ detects the stimulus.
A sensory neurone carries the impulse from the receptor to the spinal cord, with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion.
A relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord connects the sensory and motor neurones.
A motor neurone carries the impulse out to an effector, such as a muscle or gland, which responds.

questions.question: Explain how the nerve impulse is transmitted across a synapse (4 marks).
questions.answer: The impulse opens Ca2+ channels, vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, which diffuses to receptors and opens Na+ channels on the postsynaptic membrane.
steps: The action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob and depolarises its membrane.
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ diffuses into the knob.
Ca2+ causes vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na+ channels and starting a new action potential.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term sensory organ (paragraph 2 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: An organ containing sensory receptors that detect stimuli and send nerve impulses to the nervous system.
steps: A sensory receptor is a cell or structure that detects a stimulus.
A sensory organ is a group of receptors (and supporting tissue) in one structure, such as the eye or skin.
The receptors convert the stimulus into nerve impulses.
These impulses are sent to the brain or spinal cord for processing.

questions.question: Use ticks and crosses to complete the table comparing types of connective tissue in the human body, from paragraphs 3 to 7 (2 marks).
questions.answer: Fascia: contains collagen (tick), rich in nerves (tick), surrounds muscle (tick); ligaments: contains collagen (tick), rich in nerves (cross), surrounds muscle (cross).
steps: Both are fibrous connective tissues rich in collagen.
Fascia is a sheet of connective tissue wrapped round muscles and well supplied with nerve endings (pain receptors), as in the diffuse-pain paragraphs.
Ligaments join bone to bone, do not surround muscle and are poorly supplied with nerves, so the last two columns are crosses (the source text is not on the page, so this uses general knowledge).

questions.question: Describe how the fascia generates a diffuse pain (paragraphs 8 and 9 of the source) (3 marks).
