questions.answer: Inflammation releases chemical mediators that sensitise many nociceptors spread through the fascia, so impulses from a wide area are sent and the pain is poorly localised.
steps: Damage or inflammation in the fascia releases chemical mediators such as histamine and prostaglandins.
These mediators sensitise nociceptors (pain receptors) spread across the wide sheet of fascia.
Many sensory neurones send impulses to the spinal cord and brain at the same time.
The pain is felt over a wide area and is poorly localised, which is described as diffuse pain.

questions.question: Explain how inflammation in the fascia is caused (paragraphs 8 and 9 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Tissue damage releases mediators such as histamine that dilate blood vessels and make them leaky, so white blood cells and fluid enter the tissue, causing swelling and pain.
steps: Tissue damage or infection causes cells in the fascia to release inflammatory mediators such as histamine.
The mediators cause vasodilation and increase the permeability of capillaries.
Plasma proteins and white blood cells move into the surrounding tissue.
The fluid and cells cause swelling, redness and heat, which is inflammation.

questions.question: Describe how fibroblasts within the fascia could be transformed into myofibroblasts (paragraph 13 of the source) (4 marks).
questions.answer: Mechanical stress or signalling molecules such as TGF-beta activate signalling pathways that switch on genes for contractile proteins (actin), changing the fibroblast into a contractile myofibroblast.
steps: Mechanical stress on the tissue or signalling molecules such as TGF-beta bind to receptors on the fibroblast.
This starts a signal transduction pathway inside the cell.
Transcription factors switch on genes for contractile proteins such as alpha-smooth muscle actin.
The fibroblast develops a contractile cytoskeleton and becomes a myofibroblast.

questions.question: Explain how lymph is moved in one direction in the lymphatic system (paragraphs 15 and 16 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Valves in lymph vessels prevent backflow, and contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes the vessels to push lymph forward.
steps: Lymph vessels contain valves that open only in the direction of lymph flow.
When skeletal muscles contract they squeeze the lymph vessels, raising the pressure of the lymph.
The valves close when the pressure pushes backwards, so lymph cannot flow back.
Lymph therefore moves forward towards the veins, where it re-enters the blood.

questions.question: Suggest how ageing may have an adverse effect on the structure of the lymphatic system (paragraph 17 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Ageing can make lymph vessel walls stiffer and less elastic, damage the valves and reduce lymph node tissue, so lymph flow is impaired.
steps: With age, the walls of lymph vessels become thicker and less elastic.
Valves in the vessels may weaken or become less effective, allowing backflow.
The number and function of lymph nodes can decline with age.
As a result, lymph flow is slowed and the structure of the system is impaired.

questions.question: How many of three statements about serotonin are correct? Statements: L-dopa can be converted into serotonin in the brain; serotonin is a neurotransmitter; serotonin is produced by post-synaptic neurones. A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3 (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - one statement is correct.
steps: L-dopa is converted into dopamine, not serotonin, so statement 1 is wrong.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter released at synapses, so statement 2 is correct.
Serotonin is made and released by presynaptic neurones, not post-synaptic neurones, so statement 3 is wrong.
One statement is correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Explain how three genes can produce 14 different serotonin receptors (4 marks).
questions.answer: Alternative splicing of the mRNA from each gene joins different combinations of exons, so one gene can produce several different receptor proteins.
steps: Each gene is transcribed into a pre-mRNA containing exons and introns.
During RNA processing, introns are removed and exons are joined in different combinations (alternative splicing).
Different mRNA molecules from the same gene therefore code for different polypeptide sequences.
Each different mRNA is translated into a different receptor protein, giving many more receptor types than genes.

questions.question: Determine the effect of MDMA on the serotonin level in cerebrospinal fluid, using the graph (2 marks).
questions.answer: Increasing the MDMA dose increases the serotonin concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid (about 265 to 390 mg cm^-3 from 0 to 15 mg kg^-1).
steps: The line of best fit rises throughout, showing a positive relationship: serotonin is about 265 mg cm^-3 with no MDMA and about 385 to 390 mg cm^-3 at 15 mg kg^-1, an increase of nearly 50 %.
The results are not perfectly linear (330 at 5 mg kg^-1 and 320 at 10 mg kg^-1) but overall serotonin is higher at every dose than with no MDMA.

questions.question: Predict the serotonin concentration for a dose of 17.5 mg per kg MDMA, using the line of best fit, in g cm-3 (2 marks).
questions.answer: About 0.41 g cm^-3 (about 410 mg cm^-3)
steps: Use the line of best fit: it rises from about 265 mg cm^-3 at 0 to about 385 mg cm^-3 at 15 mg kg^-1, a gradient of about 8 mg cm^-3 per mg kg^-1.
Extend it by 2.5 mg kg^-1 beyond 15: 385 + 2.5 x 8 = about 405 to 410 mg cm^-3.
Convert mg to g by dividing by 1000: 0.41 g cm^-3 (accept 0.40 to 0.41).

questions.question: Explain how MDMA taken by mouth could affect the level of serotonin in the brain, using the information in the question (3 marks).
questions.answer: MDMA is absorbed from the gut into the blood, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and increases serotonin release or blocks its reuptake, raising serotonin levels.
steps: MDMA taken by mouth is absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
It is carried in the blood and crosses the blood-brain barrier into the brain.
In the brain it increases release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks serotonin reuptake transporters.
Serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft longer, so the serotonin level in the brain rises.

questions.question: Comment on the results shown in the bar chart of dopamine release in rats given different sucrose concentrations, and how they support the conclusion (4 marks).
questions.answer: Dopamine release rises as sucrose concentration rises (about 21 %, 33 % and 50 % at 0.03, 0.10 and 0.30 mol dm^-3), which supports the conclusion, but the overlapping error bars make the differences between concentrations uncertain.
steps: Dopamine increased at every concentration and the lower end of every error bar is above 0 %, so drinking sucrose does increase dopamine release.
The increase is greater at higher concentrations (about 21, 33 and 50 %), so more sucrose gives a bigger effect and a greater desire to eat if dopamine drives that desire.
The error bars overlap (e.g. 0.03: about 10 to 33 %, 0.10: about 14 to 51 %), so the differences between concentrations may not be significant.
No control with no sucrose or sample size is shown, and eating itself was not measured, so the conclusion is only indirectly supported.

questions.question: Complete the table to calculate the standard deviation of the results for sucrose at 0.4 mol dm-3, giving the answer to two significant figures (2 marks).
steps: Mean = (45 + 63 + 74 + 58) / 4 = 60, so the missing x - mean value for 58 is -2 and its square is 4.

questions.question: Describe the role of adrenaline in the fight or flight response (3 marks).
questions.answer: Adrenaline binds receptors on target cells, raising heart rate and breakdown of glycogen to glucose, and redirecting blood flow to the muscles.
steps: Adrenaline is released into the blood from the adrenal medulla when a person is stressed.
It binds to receptors on target cells, such as heart muscle and liver cells.
In the liver and muscles it activates glycogen breakdown, releasing glucose for respiration.
It increases heart rate and stroke volume and redirects blood flow to the skeletal muscles, preparing the body for action.

questions.question: Discuss how negative feedback is involved in controlling blood glucose concentration, using the diagram and graphs of daily changes in insulin, glucagon and glucose (6 marks).
questions.answer: Blood glucose is kept within narrow limits by negative feedback: a high level causes insulin release which lowers it, and a low level causes glucagon release which raises it.
steps: High blood glucose is detected by the pancreas, which releases insulin; insulin stimulates tissue cells to take up glucose and the liver to form glycogen, so blood glucose falls back to normal.

The graphs show insulin peaks (about 48, 43 and 40 units cm^-3) just after each rise in glucose following meals, and glucose then falls back from 108, 118 and 125 mg per 100 cm^3 to about 100, so the rise is reversed.

When glucose falls (e.g. overnight, about 90 mg per 100 cm^3) insulin falls to about 10 and glucagon is slightly higher (about 1.3 to 1.6 ng cm^-3); glucagon stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver, raising blood glucose.
Each hormone's release is stopped by the effect it produces, so glucose stays within about 90 to 125 mg per 100 cm^3 all day, despite meals, which shows negative feedback.

questions.question: The actual length of the brain shown on the MRI scan is 15 cm. Calculate the actual diameter, in mm, of the lesion between X and Y (2 marks).
questions.answer: About 20 mm (accept 18 to 22 mm)
steps: Measure the length of the brain on the scan (top to bottom) and the distance X to Y: X to Y is about 0.13 of the brain length.
Actual diameter = 0.133 x 15 cm = 2.0 cm.
Convert to millimetres: 2.0 cm x 10 = 20 mm.

questions.question: Show that the effect of axon diameter on conduction speed is six times greater in a myelinated neurone than in a non-myelinated neurone, using the table (2 marks).
questions.answer: Doubling the diameter from 1 to 2 um raises the myelinated speed by about 227 % but the non-myelinated speed by only 35 %, about six times greater.
steps: Myelinated: speed rises from 2.6 to 8.5 m s^-1, an increase of 5.9 m s^-1, which is 5.9 / 2.6 x 100 = 227 %.
Non-myelinated: speed rises from 2.3 to 3.1 m s^-1, an increase of 0.8 m s^-1, which is 0.8 / 2.3 x 100 = 35 %.
Ratio = 227 / 35 = 6.5, so diameter has roughly six times the effect in myelinated neurones (in absolute terms the increase is 5.9 / 0.8 = 7.4 times).

questions.question: Explain the effect of the myelin sheath and of the axon diameter on the speed of conduction of an impulse (4 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin allows saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier, and a larger axon diameter reduces resistance to the flow of ions, so both increase conduction speed.
steps: Myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier.
The impulse jumps between nodes (saltatory conduction), which is faster than continuous conduction.
A larger axon diameter has less resistance to the flow of ions along the axon, so local currents spread further.
Larger diameters therefore increase conduction speed, and the effect is larger when the axon is myelinated.

questions.question: Suggest why a person with MS could have blindness in one eye and lack of coordination (3 marks).
questions.answer: Demyelination of the optic nerve stops impulses from the eye reaching the brain, and lesions in the cerebellum disrupt coordination of movement.
steps: MS destroys myelin in the central nervous system, forming lesions.
Demyelination of the optic nerve from one eye slows or blocks impulses, so vision in that eye is lost.
Lesions in the cerebellum or brain pathways disrupt the coordination of movements.
Impulses for balance and movement are therefore poorly timed, causing lack of coordination.

questions.question: In an investigation with 350 insects, calculate the mean decrease in the number of insects showing PER each time the procedure was repeated, using the graph (3 marks).
questions.answer: About 6 insects per repeat
steps: At the start 100 % of the 350 insects show PER, and by about 58 repeats none do, so the total decrease is 350 insects.
Mean decrease per repeat = 350 / 58 = 6.0 insects each time.

questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation into the proboscis extension response to a heat stimulus (3 marks).
questions.answer: The insects show habituation: the heat pad is repeatedly presented with no reward, so they learn to ignore it and fewer extend the proboscis each time.
steps: The percentage showing the proboscis extension response falls from 100 % to 0 % as the procedure is repeated 58 times, so the response is lost with repeated exposure to the same stimulus.
This is habituation: the warm stimulus repeatedly gives no food, so the nervous system stops responding (fewer neurotransmitter vesicles released at the synapse).
It avoids wasting energy responding to an unimportant stimulus; the small ups and downs in the curve are natural variation.

questions.question: Suggest why a drop in the PER to a heat stimulus could be an advantage to these insects (2 marks).
questions.answer: Habituation to a harmless heat stimulus stops wasteful feeding attempts, saving energy and avoiding unnecessary bites.
steps: Heat from a heat pad or other non-host source is not a sign of a host, so extending the proboscis wastes time.
If the insect habituates, it stops responding to repeated harmless heat stimuli.
This saves energy that would otherwise be spent on unnecessary proboscis extension.
The insect can concentrate its feeding on real hosts and avoid exposing itself to predators.

questions.question: Name the main type of muscle fibre used in the leg muscles of a sprinter (1 mark).
questions.answer: Fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibres.
steps: Sprinting needs rapid, powerful contractions over a short time.
Fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and generate high force.
They rely more on anaerobic respiration, so they produce lactate.
So the main fibre type is fast-twitch (type II).

questions.question: During a sprint, leg muscles produce lactate. Describe what happens to the lactate at the end of the race (3 marks).
questions.answer: Lactate is carried in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back to pyruvate and used to make glucose or to be oxidised, while oxygen debt is repaid.
steps: Anaerobic respiration in the muscles produces lactate when oxygen is insufficient.
Lactate diffuses into the blood and is carried to the liver.
In the liver it is converted back to pyruvate, which can be used to make glucose (gluconeogenesis) or be oxidised.
Extra oxygen taken in after exercise is used to repay the oxygen debt and oxidise the lactate.

questions.question: Which statements are features of muscle fibres in a long-distance runner? 1 reduced blood capillary network, 2 larger number of mitochondria, 3 low concentration of myoglobin. A 1 only, B 2 only, C 1 and 3 only, D 2 and 3 only (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - 2 only (more mitochondria).
steps: Long-distance runners need a good blood supply, so their muscle fibres have a dense capillary network, making statement 1 wrong.
Aerobic endurance needs many mitochondria to produce ATP, so statement 2 is correct.
Myoglobin stores oxygen, so endurance fibres have a high (not low) concentration of it; statement 3 is wrong.
Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Which of the following explains how muscles contract? A Fick's law, B fluid mosaic model, C lock and key hypothesis, D sliding filament model (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - sliding filament model.
steps: The sliding filament model describes how actin and myosin filaments slide past each other to shorten the sarcomere.
Fick's law describes diffusion rates, not muscle contraction.
The fluid mosaic model describes the structure of cell membranes.
The lock and key hypothesis describes enzyme action, so the answer is D.

questions.question: Discuss the differences between athletes and non-athletes in two investigations, using the table of measurements and the graph of power against oxygen used (6 marks).
questions.answer: Athletes have a lower resting heart rate and a greater capacity to use oxygen (aerobically and anaerobically), and reach higher power outputs, but at a given power they use oxygen at a similar rate to non-athletes.
steps: Table: resting heart rate is lower in athletes (66 against 71 bpm) as their stronger hearts have a bigger stroke volume; peak heart rate is slightly lower (190 against 196), so the heart does not need to beat as fast.

Maximum oxygen use is much higher in athletes under aerobic conditions (57 against 39 cm^3 kg^-1 min^-1, +46 %) and anaerobic (35 against 20, +75 %), because of more mitochondria, more capillaries and myoglobin in muscles and more efficient lungs and blood supply.

Graph: in both groups oxygen use rises with power generated (positive correlation), and the two sets of points overlap between about 2.5 and 3.5 W kg^-1, so at the same power the oxygen cost is similar.
Athletes reach higher power (up to about 5.0 against about 3.7 W kg^-1) and oxygen use (up to about 64 against about 51), so they can sustain greater exercise.
The samples are small (n = 11 and 10), so the differences may not be significant and other factors such as age and sex are not given.

questions.question: Which labelled part of the brain section contains the cardiovascular control centre? A P, B Q, C R, D S (1 mark)
questions.answer: A: P (medulla oblongata)
steps: P points to the lower part of the brainstem, the medulla oblongata, which contains the cardiovascular and respiratory control centres.
Q is the pituitary gland, R the hypothalamus, S the cerebral hemisphere and T the cerebellum.

questions.question: Which labelled part of the brain section would control balance and coordinate movement? A P, B Q, C R, D T (1 mark)
questions.answer: D: T (cerebellum)
steps: The cerebellum, at the back and below the cerebral hemispheres (label T), controls balance and coordinates movement.
P is the medulla oblongata, Q the pituitary and R the hypothalamus.

questions.question: Which labelled parts of the brain section would be involved in controlling the solute concentration of blood plasma? A P and Q, B Q and R, C P and R, D S and T (1 mark)
questions.answer: B: Q and R (pituitary gland and hypothalamus)
steps: The hypothalamus (R) has osmoreceptors that detect the solute concentration of the blood and makes ADH.
The pituitary gland (Q) releases ADH, which alters the kidney's reabsorption of water and so the plasma concentration, so B is correct.

questions.question: Which statement about dopamine is correct? A it can pass from the bloodstream into neurones, B it is a neurotransmitter, C high levels are linked to depression, D low levels cause breakdown of myelin (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - dopamine is a neurotransmitter.
steps: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter released by neurones to pass impulses across synapses.
It cannot pass from the blood into neurones, as it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so A is wrong.
Low dopamine is linked to Parkinson's disease and depression, not high levels, so C is wrong.
Low dopamine does not cause breakdown of myelin, so D is wrong.

questions.question: Explain why selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs), which affect reabsorption of serotonin at synapses, can be used to treat depression (3 marks).
questions.answer: SSRIs block reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer and stimulates postsynaptic receptors more, improving mood.
steps: Serotonin is released into the synaptic cleft and normally reabsorbed by the presynaptic neurone through transporters.
SSRIs block these serotonin transporters, so reabsorption is reduced.
Serotonin remains in the synapse longer and binds to postsynaptic receptors for longer.
Increased serotonin signalling is thought to improve mood in depression.

questions.question: Give a definition for the term sarcopenia (paragraph 1 of the source) (1 mark).
questions.answer: The age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and function.
steps: Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass that occurs with ageing.
It also involves loss of muscle strength and function.
It is caused by reduced muscle fibre number and size.
It increases the risk of falls and reduced mobility in older people.

questions.question: Explain how a specialised cell such as a muscle cell is produced from a stem cell (paragraph 2 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: The stem cell divides, and transcription factors switch on the genes for muscle proteins so the cell differentiates into a specialised muscle cell.
steps: The stem cell divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells.
Signals from the environment cause transcription factors to be activated in some daughter cells.
These transcription factors switch on the genes for muscle-specific proteins such as myosin and actin.
The cell differentiates into a specialised muscle cell that contains those proteins.

questions.question: Describe how reduced production of testosterone in the testes can result in reduced muscle protein (paragraph 5 of the source) (4 marks).
questions.answer: Less testosterone means less hormone-receptor complex binds DNA, so fewer genes for muscle proteins are transcribed and less protein is synthesised.
steps: Testosterone is a steroid hormone produced by the testes that diffuses through the muscle cell membrane.
It binds to intracellular androgen receptors, forming a hormone-receptor complex.
The complex acts as a transcription factor that binds to DNA and switches on genes for muscle proteins.
With less testosterone, less transcription occurs, so less muscle protein is synthesised.

questions.question: Explain how negative feedback can maintain a system within a narrow limit, using insulin control of blood glucose as the example (2 marks).
questions.answer: A change from the set point is detected and the response reverses the change, so the system returns to the narrow range.
steps: A receptor detects a deviation from the set point, such as a rise in blood glucose.
The control system triggers a response, such as insulin release, which reverses the change.
As the level returns to normal, the stimulus for the response is removed.
So the level stays within a narrow range around the set point.

questions.question: Suggest how insulin increases the uptake of glucose by muscle cells (paragraph 7 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Insulin binds receptors on muscle cells, causing GLUT4 glucose transporter vesicles to move to the membrane, so more glucose enters the cells.
steps: Insulin binds to specific receptors on the muscle cell surface membrane.
This triggers signalling that moves vesicles containing GLUT4 glucose transporters to the membrane.
The transporters fuse with the membrane, so more glucose can enter by facilitated diffusion.
More glucose is taken up, so blood glucose falls.

questions.question: Describe how computed tomography (CT) scans can be used to measure increases in muscle size in older individuals (paragraph 9 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: CT scans give cross-sectional images of the muscle, so the cross-sectional area of the muscle can be measured and compared before and after exercise.
steps: CT scans use X-rays to produce cross-sectional images of the muscle.
The muscle appears clearly against surrounding tissue because tissues absorb X-rays differently.
The cross-sectional area of the muscle is measured on the scans.
Scans taken before and after aerobic exercise are compared to show the increase in size.

questions.question: Explain why aerobic exercise increases mitochondrial density and activity (paragraph 9 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Exercise increases energy demand and signals activate genes for mitochondrial proteins, so the muscle makes more mitochondria to supply more ATP by aerobic respiration.
steps: Aerobic exercise increases the demand for ATP in the muscle fibres.
Signals from the exercise activate transcription of genes for mitochondrial proteins.
More mitochondria are made (mitochondrial biogenesis), increasing their density in the muscle.
More aerobic respiration then takes place in the mitochondria, producing more ATP for contraction.

questions.question: Explain why diets rich in whey and egg protein may not be ideal for prolonged treatment of a protein-poor diet (paragraph 11 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Whey and egg protein are digested and absorbed quickly, so amino acid levels rise and fall rapidly, and excess amino acids are broken down and excreted as urea, so prolonged high-protein intake is not efficient and puts extra work on the liver and kidneys.
steps: These proteins are absorbed rapidly, so the supply of amino acids to muscle is short-lived rather than steady.
In older people muscle responds less to amino acids (anabolic resistance), so extra protein alone does not keep building muscle without exercise.

Amino acids not used for protein synthesis are deaminated in the liver and the nitrogen is excreted as urea, which over a long period increases the load on the kidneys (the source paragraph is not on the page, so this uses general knowledge).

questions.question: Which receptors detect a change in light intensity and stimulate an action potential? A baroreceptors, B chemoreceptors, C osmoreceptors, D photoreceptors (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - photoreceptors.
steps: Photoreceptors are receptor cells that detect light, in the retina of the eye.
A change in light intensity changes their membrane potential and triggers action potentials.
Baroreceptors detect pressure, chemoreceptors detect chemicals and osmoreceptors detect water potential.
So the correct answer is D, photoreceptors.

questions.question: Describe the structures a nerve impulse passes through from receptors in the skin to the central nervous system in a human reflex arc (3 marks).
questions.answer: Receptor in the skin, sensory neurone with cell body in the dorsal root ganglion, dorsal root of the spinal nerve, and into the grey matter of the spinal cord.
steps: The stimulus is detected by a receptor (such as a touch or pain receptor) in the skin.
The impulse travels along a sensory neurone, whose cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion.
The impulse enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root of the spinal nerve.
It then passes to a relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, before the CNS processes it.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage difference between the number of roundworms in group 1 and group 2 that changed direction 30 minutes after habituation (2 marks), using the graph.
steps: At 30 minutes group 1 has 20 roundworms changing direction and group 2 has 12.
Difference = 20 - 12 = 8 and mean = (20 + 12) / 2 = 16.
Percentage difference = 8 / 16 x 100 = 50 %.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions about recovery times after habituation, using the graph of results (3 marks).
questions.answer: Recovery increases with time after habituation in all groups; it is greatest after habituation with short intervals between taps (group 1) and least after the longest intervals (group 3); recovery is fastest in the first 10 minutes.
steps: At 0 and 0.5 minutes no roundworm responded in any group, and the number changing direction rises with time, so the response recovers gradually after habituation.
The shorter the interval between taps during habituation, the quicker the recovery: at 30 minutes group 1 (2 s intervals) had 20 responding, group 2 (10 s) had 12 and group 3 (60 s) only 4.
Most recovery happens in the first 10 minutes (to 17, 7 and 2) and the rate slows after that, and no group has fully recovered (maximum 20 of 25) by 30 minutes.

questions.question: Which feature of pronghorns is an adaptation for running long distances at high speeds? A decreased glomerular filtration rate, B increased number of slow twitch muscle fibres, C narrower airways, D smaller cardiac output (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - increased number of slow twitch muscle fibres.
steps: Slow twitch fibres are fatigue-resistant and use aerobic respiration, so they suit long-distance running.
A decreased glomerular filtration rate and a smaller cardiac output would reduce the supply of oxygen and blood to muscles, which is not an advantage.
Narrower airways would increase resistance to airflow and reduce gas exchange during running.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Explain how the heart rate and ventilation rate of a pronghorn are increased to enable it to run long distances at high speeds (4 marks).
questions.answer: Adrenaline and sympathetic impulses increase SAN firing and heart rate; rising CO2 is detected by chemoreceptors, which increase breathing rate and depth via the medulla.
steps: Running activates the sympathetic nervous system, and adrenaline is released into the blood.
Sympathetic impulses and adrenaline increase the rate of firing of the SAN, so heart rate rises.
Muscles produce more CO2, which is detected by chemoreceptors that send impulses to the medulla.
The medulla increases the rate of impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so ventilation rate and depth increase.

questions.question: Describe the relationships between mass, resting metabolic rate and pulse rate shown in the table of five mammals (3 marks).
questions.answer: As mass increases, resting metabolic rate increases but pulse rate decreases; metabolic rate per kg falls with increasing mass.
steps: Resting metabolic rate rises with mass, from 1.45 J s^-1 in the 0.26 kg rat to 267 J s^-1 in the 400 kg cow, but less than proportionally: the cow is about 1500 times heavier but its rate is only about 180 times greater.
Pulse rate falls as mass increases, from 420 bpm in the rat to 40 bpm in the cow (rat > dog > sheep, with the human at 72 bpm slightly above the sheep at 70 bpm, despite being heavier).

Small mammals have a higher metabolic rate per kg (5.6 J s^-1 kg^-1 for the rat against 0.67 for the cow) and a faster heart rate to supply oxygen, because of their larger surface area to volume ratio and greater heat loss.

questions.question: Describe how the body temperature of a human is maintained at 37 C during exercise, when metabolic rate increases and heat is released (3 marks).
questions.answer: Sweating allows evaporation to lose heat, and vasodilation of skin arterioles increases heat loss, under control of the hypothalamus.
steps: The hypothalamus detects a rise in blood temperature and acts as the thermoregulatory centre.
It sends impulses to sweat glands, which secrete sweat that evaporates from the skin, removing heat.
Arterioles in the skin vasodilate, so more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost by radiation.
Heat loss balances the heat produced by respiration, so body temperature stays at 37 C.

questions.question: A section of squirrel monkey retina contains 5000 photoreceptors. Calculate how many would be rod cells, assuming an even distribution (2 marks), using the table of photoreceptor numbers.
questions.answer: About 4170 rod cells (4.17 x 10^3, about 4200)
steps: Squirrel monkey: 7.0 x 10^6 cones and 3.5 x 10^7 rods, so total = 4.2 x 10^7 photoreceptors.
Fraction that are rods = 3.5 x 10^7 / 4.2 x 10^7 = 0.833.
Rods in 5000 photoreceptors = 5000 x 0.833 = 4170.

questions.question: Explain why there is a difference in the numbers of rod cells and cone cells in the retinas of the grey-bellied night monkey and the squirrel monkey (3 marks).
questions.answer: The night monkey is active in low light so has many rod cells for sensitivity, while the squirrel monkey is active in daylight and has many cone cells for colour vision at high light intensity.
steps: Rod cells are sensitive to low light intensities and do not give colour vision.
Cone cells need higher light intensities and give colour vision.
The grey-bellied night monkey is active at night, so it needs many rod cells to see in dim light.
The squirrel monkey is active in the day, so it has more cone cells for colour vision and detailed sight in bright light.

questions.question: Deduce the effect of each treatment on seedlings that have had their apical buds removed, using the table of treatments and their appearance after exposure to light (3 marks).
questions.answer: Auxin applied to the cut top keeps the lateral buds from growing (restores apical dominance) and the shoot bends towards the light; gibberellin makes the stem longer but does not prevent lateral growth or cause bending; without treatment the lateral buds grow out.
steps: Seedling 1 (no treatment): with the apical bud gone there is no auxin from the tip, so the lateral buds grow out into shoots, showing apical dominance has been lost.

Seedling 2 (auxin): the lateral buds stay small, so auxin replaces the apical bud's effect in inhibiting lateral buds, and the stem bends towards the light because auxin moves to the shaded side and makes it elongate more.

Seedling 3 (gibberellin): the stem is taller with longer internodes, so gibberellin stimulates stem elongation; the shoot stays upright and the lateral buds are not inhibited, so gibberellin does not restore apical dominance or cause phototropism.

questions.question: Explain why the symptoms of Parkinson's disease increase with age, using the graph of the number of dopamine-producing cells against age (4 marks).
questions.answer: Dopamine-producing cells die progressively, so the number falls with age; the fewer cells there are, the less dopamine is made and the worse the movement symptoms become.
steps: In the graph the number falls from 500 000 at age 10 to about 385 000 at 40, 300 000 at 50, 150 000 at 60 and only about 20 000 at 80, with the steepest fall after 40.
People without Parkinson's rarely fall below 350 000 cells, so below this level (reached at about 45 years) there is not enough dopamine and symptoms appear.

Less dopamine is released at synapses, so there is less stimulation of the neurones that control movement (e.g. in the basal ganglia), causing tremor and slow movement; as cells continue to die the symptoms get worse.

questions.question: Suggest why carbidopa, an inhibitor of the enzyme in the digestive system, is given with L-DOPA tablets (2 marks).
questions.answer: Carbidopa stops L-DOPA being converted to dopamine in the gut, so more L-DOPA reaches the brain and fewer side effects occur.
steps: L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by an enzyme (decarboxylase) found in the digestive system as well as in the brain.
If dopamine is made in the gut, it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so it is wasted.
Carbidopa inhibits the enzyme in the digestive system, so more L-DOPA stays intact.
More L-DOPA then crosses into the brain to be converted to dopamine, and dopamine in the gut (causing side effects such as nausea) is reduced.

questions.question: Comment on the results of an investigation in which different concentrations of dopamine were given to Drosophila, showing their mean heart rates (4 marks), using the graph.
questions.answer: Dopamine raises the heart rate of Drosophila at moderate concentrations (to about 415 beats per minute) but a very high concentration lowers it (to about 377).
steps: At log10 0, 1 and 2 the mean heart rate is about 393, 392 and 397 beats per minute with overlapping error bars, so low concentrations have little or no effect.

At log10 3 and 4 it rises to about 415 and 416 bpm, a plateau about 5 to 6 % above the low-concentration values, and the error bars do not overlap those at low concentration, so dopamine has a significant effect on heart rate.
At log10 5 the heart rate drops to about 377 bpm, below all the other values, so a very high concentration inhibits the heart (it may be toxic) and the effect is not simply increasing.
There is no control without dopamine and only groups of 10 flies, so the evidence is limited.

questions.question: Draw an arrow on the neurone diagram to show the direction of a nerve impulse (1 mark).
questions.answer: An arrow drawn along the axon pointing from right to left, from the cell body and dendrite end towards the axon terminals.
steps: The impulse travels away from the cell body and dendrites (at the right, where the cell body sits) along the myelinated axon.
So the arrow along the axon points to the left, towards the branching axon terminals with synaptic knobs.

questions.question: Which is the resting potential for this neurone? A -90 mV, B -70 mV, C +48 mV, D +70 mV (1 mark) (graph not in text).
questions.answer: B: -70 mV
steps: The resting potential is the steady level before the stimulus, at the start of the trace.
The trace is flat at -70 mV from 0 to about 1.8 ms and again from 4 ms, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Which letter on the action potential graph shows where the neurone is hyperpolarised? A U, B V, C W, D X (1 mark).
questions.answer: C: W
steps: Hyperpolarised means more negative than the resting potential of -70 mV.
W is at the bottom of the trace, about -90 mV at 3 ms, after the spike (U is the rising depolarisation, V the peak and X the return to resting), so it is C.

questions.question: What is the difference in membrane potential between points V and W on the graph? A 40 mV, B 50 mV, C 90 mV, D 140 mV (1 mark).
questions.answer: D: 140 mV
steps: V is the peak of the action potential at +50 mV and W is the trough at about -90 mV.
Difference = 50 - (-90) = 140 mV.

questions.question: Give two differences between the functions of a motor neurone and a sensory neurone (2 marks).
questions.answer: A sensory neurone carries impulses from receptors to the CNS; a motor neurone carries impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles or glands.
steps: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors towards the central nervous system.
Motor neurones carry impulses away from the central nervous system to effectors.
Sensory neurones detect stimuli, whereas motor neurones cause a response in muscles or glands.
So the two differences are the direction of the impulse and the type of target structure.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in BMAA per gram from the seeds of the cycad trees to the flying foxes, to two significant figures (1 mark), using the table.
steps: Increase in BMAA = 3556 - 37 = 3519 ug per gram.
Percentage increase = 3519 / 37 x 100 = 9511 %.
To 2 significant figures this is 9500 %.

questions.question: Explain the results of the graph of the flying fox population and the number of men diagnosed with ALS (4 marks).
questions.answer: As flying foxes became scarcer, the Chamorro ate fewer and took in less BMAA, so the number of men with ALS fell later; BMAA builds up in flying foxes, so eating them gave a high dose.
steps: Flying fox numbers fell from about 15 000 in 1950 to almost none by 1974, and then recovered slightly, because they were heavily hunted for food.

BMAA is found at 3556 ug per gram in flying fox fat compared with 37 ug per gram in cycad seeds, about 96 times more, so people eating the flying foxes were exposed to a high dose of the neurotoxin (it accumulates up the food chain).
ALS rose to about 138 per 100 000 men by 1965 and then fell to about 16 by 1995 as the supply of flying foxes, and so BMAA intake, declined.
The fall in ALS lags behind the fall in flying foxes by several years, as the disease takes many years to develop; the link is a correlation, which does not prove BMAA is the cause.

questions.question: Compare and contrast PET scans and CT scans used in diagnosing ALS of the brain and nervous tissue (3 marks).
questions.answer: Both produce images of the brain; PET shows metabolic activity using a radioactive tracer, while CT uses X-rays to show structure in cross-section.
steps: Both PET and CT produce images of the brain and nervous tissue without surgery.
Both involve radiation, from a radioactive tracer for PET and from X-rays for CT.
PET shows function by detecting metabolic activity (glucose uptake), so it shows how tissues are working.
CT shows structure in cross-section using differences in X-ray absorption, so it shows anatomy rather than activity.

questions.question: Draw a myelinated motor neurone and label two structures (3 marks).
questions.answer: A drawing of a motor neurone with a cell body (nucleus) and dendrites at one end, a long axon wrapped in myelin sheath segments with gaps (nodes of Ranvier) between, and axon terminals at the other end; two labelled structures, such as the myelin sheath and the node of Ranvier.
steps: Draw the cell body with a nucleus and short branching dendrites at one end.
Draw one long axon leaving the cell body, covered by a series of separate myelin (Schwann cell) sections with small gaps between them, ending in branched axon terminals (synaptic knobs).
Label two structures correctly with lines to them, for example myelin sheath (Schwann cell), node of Ranvier, axon, cell body or axon terminal.

questions.question: Explain how tetrodotoxin inhibits the transmission of a nerve impulse along an axon (3 marks).
questions.answer: TTX blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, so Na+ cannot enter the axon, depolarisation does not occur and no action potential is propagated.
steps: TTX binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the axon membrane.
Na+ cannot diffuse into the axon, so the membrane is not depolarised.
Without depolarisation, the threshold is not reached and no action potential is generated.
So the impulse is not transmitted along the axon, as seen by the absence of a change in potential difference.

questions.question: Which structure is the anterior cruciate ligament attached to? A bone, B cartilage, C muscle, D tendon (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - bone.
steps: Ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint, stabilising it.
The anterior cruciate ligament runs inside the knee joint between the femur and tibia.
Tendons connect muscle to bone, so D is wrong; cartilage covers bone surfaces, so B is wrong.
So the answer is A, bone.

questions.question: Describe how MRI can show damage to the anterior cruciate ligament (2 marks).
questions.answer: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to align hydrogen nuclei, and damaged ligament tissue gives a different signal, so the damage appears as a different contrast on the image.
steps: A strong magnetic field aligns the hydrogen nuclei (protons) in the tissue.
Radio waves are applied, and the nuclei emit radio signals as they return to alignment.
Damaged ligament contains different amounts of water and tissue structure, giving a different signal.
The computer builds an image in which the damaged area shows a different contrast from healthy tissue.

questions.question: There were 77 ACL repairs per 100 000 males in one year. The population was 67 000 000 and 56% were female. Calculate the number of ACL repairs in males that year (2 marks).
steps: Males are 100% - 56% = 44% of the population.
Repairs per male = 77 / 100 000 = 0.00077.
Repairs in males = 29 480 000 x 0.00077 = 22 699.6, which is about 22 700.

questions.question: Name the two types of skeletal muscle that are contracted when the arm is held in the position shown in the diagram of arm muscles (1 mark).
questions.answer: A flexor (the biceps) and an extensor (the triceps), an antagonistic pair that both contract to hold the position
steps: Holding the arm bent, the biceps (flexor, labelled B on the front) contracts to keep the elbow flexed.
The triceps (extensor, labelled A at the back) also contracts, acting against it to stabilise the joint, so the two antagonistic muscles hold the position.

questions.question: Describe how the arm could be straightened by the muscles labelled A and B in the diagram (2 marks).
questions.answer: The triceps (A) contracts while the biceps (B) relaxes, so the triceps pulls the forearm bone and the elbow straightens.
steps: The muscles are an antagonistic pair: the triceps (A, extensor) contracts and shortens, pulling on its tendon attached to the ulna.
The biceps (B, flexor) relaxes at the same time, so it does not resist and the lower arm is straightened about the elbow joint.

questions.question: Which is a function of gibberellins in plants? A hydrolyse starch to release glucose, B inhibit elongation of cells, C regulate the translation of DNA, D regulate the transcription of genes (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - regulate the transcription of genes.
steps: Gibberellins act by binding receptors and releasing DELLA repression, which allows transcription factors to switch genes on.
So they regulate transcription of genes, such as those for amylase and cell elongation.
Gibberellins promote cell elongation, so B is wrong.
Gibberellins do not hydrolyse starch or regulate translation directly, so A and C are wrong.

questions.question: Which is produced by an animal in a fight or flight response? A adenine, B adrenaline, C amylopectin, D antihypertensive (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - adrenaline.
steps: The fight or flight response is driven by adrenaline released from the adrenal medulla.
Adenine is a base in DNA and ATP, not a stress hormone.
Amylopectin is a component of starch, and antihypertensive drugs lower blood pressure.
So the answer is B, adrenaline.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions from the investigation of TBT's effect on blood testosterone and oestradiol in male mice, using the graphs (3 marks).
questions.answer: TBT lowers the testosterone concentration in a dose-dependent way; oestradiol rises at 25 and 50 mg kg^-1 but falls below the control at 100 mg kg^-1; so TBT disrupts hormone levels.
steps: Testosterone falls as TBT concentration rises: about 370 pg cm^-3 with no TBT, then 330, 275 and about 97 at 100 mg kg^-1, a fall of about 74 %, with a clear difference at 100.

Oestradiol is about 112 pg cm^-3 in the control, rises to about 142 at 25 and 163 at 50 mg kg^-1 (a significant rise at 50, as the error bars do not overlap the control), then falls to about 70 at 100 mg kg^-1, below the control.

So TBT alters the balance of steroid hormones in male mice (it is an endocrine disruptor), reducing testosterone at higher doses; the 25 mg kg^-1 results overlap the control, so are not clearly different.

questions.question: Describe how steroid hormones regulate gene transcription (3 marks).
questions.answer: The lipid-soluble steroid diffuses through the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor; the hormone-receptor complex binds DNA and switches on transcription of target genes.
steps: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, so they diffuse through the cell surface membrane.
They bind to a specific intracellular receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
The hormone-receptor complex moves to the nucleus and binds to a specific site on DNA, acting as a transcription factor.
This switches on transcription of the target gene, so mRNA and then the protein are made.

questions.question: Which row shows the events that happen during depolarisation of a neurone? (1 mark) (table not in text)
questions.answer: D: sodium channels open, membrane potential increasing
steps: During depolarisation voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ enters the axon.
The inside of the membrane becomes less negative, so the membrane potential is increasing, which is row D.

questions.question: Explain what happens during repolarisation in a neurone (3 marks).
questions.answer: Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ diffuses out and the membrane becomes negative again.
steps: At the peak of the action potential, voltage-gated Na+ channels close.
Voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ ions diffuse out of the axon.
The loss of positive charge makes the inside of the membrane negative again.
The membrane potential returns towards its resting value, ready for the next action potential.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the photograph of a cross-section of part of a sciatic nerve, in standard form (2 marks).
steps: Measure the scale bar on the photograph: about 11.7 mm.
Convert the real length to the same unit: 50.0 um = 0.0500 mm.
Magnification = image length / real length = 11.7 / 0.0500 = 234, so about 2.3 x 10^2 in standard form (accept about 2.2 to 2.5 x 10^2).

questions.question: Name a type of microscope that would be used to obtain the image of the sciatic nerve cross-section (1 mark).
questions.answer: A light (optical) microscope
steps: The image is a stained cross-section of the whole nerve at a modest magnification (about x230) with colour or grey tone from staining, which is what a light microscope gives.
An electron microscope would show much finer detail at far higher magnification.

questions.question: Explain how myelinated neurones enable a greater speed of transmission in a neurone (3 marks).
questions.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), with fewer depolarisations needed, so transmission is faster.
steps: Myelin is an electrical insulator, so ions cannot flow across the membrane under the sheath.
Depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier.
Local currents spread between the nodes, so the impulse jumps from node to node.
Fewer depolarisations are needed along the axon, so transmission is faster than in a non-myelinated neurone.

questions.question: Label the diagram of a cross-section of the human brain to show the pituitary gland (P), cerebellum (C) and hypothalamus (H) (3 marks).
questions.answer: C: the cauliflower-like structure behind and below the cerebral hemispheres; P: the small drop-shaped gland hanging at the base of the brain; H: the region just above P, below the thalamus.
steps: Label C on the cerebellum, the folded rounded structure at the back of the brain.
Label P on the small teardrop-shaped pituitary gland attached to the underside of the brain near the centre.
Label H on the hypothalamus, immediately above the pituitary and below the thalamus.

questions.question: Complete the table to show one function of each of the brain parts P, C and H (3 marks).
questions.answer: Hypothalamus: regulates body temperature and water balance (and controls the pituitary); medulla oblongata: controls heart rate and breathing rate; pituitary gland: releases hormones such as ADH and growth hormone.
steps: Hypothalamus: homeostatic control, for example detects blood solute concentration and body temperature and makes ADH.
Medulla oblongata: involuntary control of heart rate, breathing rate and blood pressure.
Pituitary gland: secretes hormones (ADH, growth hormone and others) that control other glands and the kidney.

questions.question: Describe how an action potential is produced in an axon (4 marks).
questions.answer: Stimulation opens voltage-gated Na+ channels so Na+ enters and depolarises the membrane; then K+ channels open, K+ leaves and the membrane repolarises.
steps: A stimulus causes some voltage-gated Na+ channels to open, so Na+ enters the axon.
The inside becomes positive, depolarising the membrane to around +40 mV.
Na+ channels then close and voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ diffuses out.
The membrane repolarises and briefly hyperpolarises before the Na+/K+ pump restores the resting potential.

questions.question: Calculate the maximum rate of increase in permeability of the axon membrane to potassium ions, to two significant figures with units (2 marks), using the graph.
questions.answer: About 19 a.u. ms^-1 (accept 18 to 21)
steps: The maximum rate of increase is the steepest part of the rising curve, about 1.0 to 1.4 ms; draw a tangent there.
Between 1.0 ms (about 7.2 a.u.) and 1.4 ms (about 14.7 a.u.) the permeability rises by 7.5 a.u. over 0.4 ms.
Gradient = 7.5 / 0.4 = about 19 a.u. per millisecond (a.u. ms^-1).

questions.question: Which is the ratio of potassium ion concentration outside and inside an axon? A 0.026:1, B 0.3:1, C 0.083:1, D 30:1 (1 mark), using the table of ion concentrations.
steps: Outside K+ = 4 mol dm^-3 and inside K+ = 155 mol dm^-3.
Ratio outside : inside = 4 / 155 = 0.026, so the ratio is 0.026 : 1.

questions.question: Explain the effect of an increase in temperature on the speed of a nerve impulse along an axon (2 marks).
questions.answer: A higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of ions and the rate of diffusion and ion channel opening, so the impulse travels faster.
steps: Higher temperature gives ions and molecules more kinetic energy, so they move faster.
Ion channels and pumps open and close more quickly, so depolarisation and repolarisation happen faster.
Faster channel activity and diffusion mean an action potential is regenerated more quickly along the axon.
So the speed of the nerve impulse increases (up to a point before proteins denature).

questions.question: Describe two conclusions about the effect of axon diameter and myelination on the speed of an impulse, using the table of results for four neurones (2 marks).
questions.answer: Myelinated neurones conduct faster than non-myelinated ones of the same diameter, and a larger diameter gives a faster speed, with a bigger effect in myelinated neurones.
steps: Myelination raises speed at both diameters: A is 7.0 against B 3.8 m s^-1 at 2.5 um (about 1.8 times faster) and C is 4.0 against D 2.5 m s^-1 at 1.5 um (1.6 times).
Greater diameter raises speed: 2.5 um gives 7.0 and 3.8 m s^-1 against 4.0 and 2.5 at 1.5 um, and the effect is bigger with myelin (an increase of 3.0 m s^-1 against 1.3 m s^-1 without).

questions.question: Give one reason why optimal hydration is beneficial (paragraph 1 of the source) (1 mark).
questions.answer: It maintains blood volume and blood pressure, so the blood can carry oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
steps: Water makes up most of the blood plasma.
Adequate water keeps blood volume and blood pressure normal.
This allows efficient transport of oxygen, glucose and other substances to tissues.
It also supports thermoregulation through sweating and normal metabolic reactions.

questions.question: Explain how caffeine present in an energy drink can affect the cells of the brain (paragraphs 3 and 32 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Caffeine resembles adenosine and binds its receptors on neurones, blocking the inhibitory effect of adenosine so the neurones are more active.
steps: Caffeine has a similar shape to adenosine, a molecule that normally inhibits neurone activity.
Caffeine binds to adenosine receptors on the membranes of brain neurones without activating them.
This blocks adenosine from binding, so its inhibitory effect is prevented.
The neurones remain more active, which causes the stimulant effect.

questions.question: Explain one reason why a typical man has a larger daily requirement for water than a typical woman (paragraph 9 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Men typically have a greater body mass and more muscle, so a higher metabolic rate and greater water loss through sweating and urine.
steps: Men usually have a greater body mass and a higher proportion of muscle.
Greater mass and muscle activity mean a higher metabolic rate.
A higher metabolic rate produces more heat and water loss by sweating and breathing.
Therefore men need more water to replace these losses.

questions.question: Explain how the sodium ion concentration in the blood is kept within a narrow range (paragraph 17 of the source) (5 marks).
questions.answer: Osmoreceptors detect changes; ADH increases water reabsorption, aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the kidney tubules, and thirst increases water intake, restoring the concentration.
steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood sodium (solute) concentration.
The posterior pituitary releases more ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.
The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone, which increases sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.
Thirst increases water intake, and the blood concentration is restored to its normal narrow range by negative feedback.

questions.question: Explain why cells shrink a bit when blood electrolyte concentration increases (paragraph 21 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: The blood has a lower water potential, so water moves out of cells by osmosis, making them shrink.
steps: An increase in blood electrolyte (solute) concentration lowers the water potential of the blood.
Water moves out of the cells by osmosis, down the water potential gradient.
Cells lose water and so shrink slightly.
This is why cells are affected when the solute concentration of the blood rises.

questions.question: Suggest how a high nitrate content in beetroot juice can lead to increased blood flow to muscles (paragraph 29 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Nitrate is converted to nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle in arterioles, causing vasodilation and increased blood flow to muscles.
steps: Nitrate from beetroot juice is converted to nitrite and then to nitric oxide (NO).
Nitric oxide diffuses into the smooth muscle of arteriole walls.
It causes the smooth muscle to relax, so the arterioles dilate (vasodilation).
Blood flow to the muscles increases, supplying more oxygen during exercise.

questions.question: Describe how energy drinks could be shown to cause irregular heart rhythms (paragraph 34 of the source) (3 marks).
questions.answer: Record heart rhythm with an ECG before and after drinking, in a group given energy drink and a control group given a placebo, and compare the traces for arrhythmias.
steps: Select a group of volunteers and record a baseline ECG to measure their normal heart rhythm.
Give one group an energy drink and a control group a similar drink without caffeine.
Record ECGs at intervals after drinking and look for irregular rhythms (arrhythmias) such as extra beats.
Compare the frequency of irregular rhythms between the groups, using statistics, to see if the energy drink causes the effect.

questions.question: Explain one reason why some people are not able to tolerate cow's milk (paragraphs 30 and 31 of the source) (2 marks).
questions.answer: Some people lack the enzyme lactase, so lactose is not hydrolysed and passes to the gut, where bacteria ferment it, causing symptoms.
steps: Lactose is a disaccharide that must be hydrolysed by the enzyme lactase into glucose and galactose.
People who do not produce enough lactase cannot digest lactose.
Undigested lactose moves into the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it.
Fermentation produces gas and osmotic effects that cause the symptoms of intolerance.

questions.question: Which chemical would increase the likelihood of a nerve impulse being initiated at a post-synaptic membrane? A auxin, B dopamine, C gibberellin, D statin (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - dopamine (an excitatory neurotransmitter).
steps: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that can bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
Binding opens ion channels that depolarise the membrane, making an impulse more likely.
Auxin and gibberellin are plant growth substances and statins are cholesterol-lowering drugs, so A, C and D are not neurotransmitters.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Assess the effects of lidocaine on cell survival of heart muscle cells cultured in low oxygen, using the graph (3 marks).
questions.answer: Lidocaine increases the survival of heart muscle cells in low oxygen, and the higher the concentration the greater the survival, reaching about 96 % at 0.01 mol dm^-3, close to the control.
steps: With low oxygen and no lidocaine only about 40 % of cells survive, against 100 % in the control with excess oxygen.

Survival rises with each increase in lidocaine concentration: about 52 % at 0.0005, 67 % at 0.001, 84 % at 0.005 and 96 % at 0.01 mol dm^-3, a positive relationship with error bars that mostly do not overlap those of the 0 concentration.

At 0.01 mol dm^-3 survival is within the error bars of the control (about 100 %), so lidocaine almost completely protects the cells; the rise is smaller at higher concentrations, suggesting it levels off.

questions.question: Which describes the term myogenic? A a hormone that initiates differentiation, B cardiac muscle that can contract with no external stimulus, C how a heartbeat is initiated in the AVN, D how muscles work in pairs (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - cardiac muscle that can contract with no external stimulus.
steps: Myogenic means the muscle contracts on its own, without a nerve impulse as the trigger.
Heart muscle is myogenic because the SAN generates its own rhythm.
Option A describes a hormone, option C describes the AVN and option D describes antagonistic muscles.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Suggest how lidocaine protects heart muscle cells from the effects of low oxygen (2 marks).
questions.answer: Lidocaine blocks Na+ entry, so less Na+ enters the cells and less ATP is needed to pump it out, saving ATP and preventing cell damage when oxygen is low.
steps: In low oxygen, ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation falls.
Normally Na+ leaks in and the Na+/K+ pump uses ATP to remove it.
Lidocaine blocks the movement of Na+ through the membrane, so less Na+ enters.
Less ATP is used by the pump, so the cells keep their ion balance and survive longer.

questions.question: Discuss how exercise reduces the risk of death from cardiovascular disease, using Graph 1 (heart rate and exercise) and Graph 2 (risk of death with and without CVD) (6 marks).
questions.answer: Exercise makes the heart more efficient, with a lower heart rate for the same work, and it lowers the risk factors for CVD, so the risk of death falls as weekly exercise increases, particularly in people with CVD.
steps: Graph 1: athletes have a lower resting rate, a smaller rise during exercise and a faster return to resting rate afterwards than non-athletes, so their hearts are stronger with a larger stroke volume and are under less strain.

Graph 2: for both groups the risk of death falls as weekly exercise increases; in people without CVD it falls quickly then levels off at a low level, while for people with CVD it starts higher but keeps falling and gets close to the risk without CVD at the longest durations.

Regular exercise also lowers blood pressure and blood cholesterol (LDL), reduces the build-up of atheroma in the arteries and helps control body mass and blood glucose, so less risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and heart attack.
The graphs have no numbers, and a correlation does not show that exercise is the cause.

questions.question: Name the type of microscope that would be used to produce the image of a mitochondrion with magnification x23 500 (1 mark).
questions.answer: Transmission electron microscope (TEM).
steps: Magnifications of tens of thousands of times are only possible with electron microscopes.
Light microscopes cannot resolve organelles such as mitochondria at this magnification.
The electron microscope used to see internal structures of mitochondria is a transmission electron microscope.
So the answer is a transmission electron microscope.

questions.question: Calculate the actual width of the mitochondrion between points A and B on the photograph, in metres to three significant figures, with magnification x23 500 (2 marks).
steps: Measure the line A to B on the photograph: about 34.4 mm.
Actual width = image length / magnification = 34.4 mm / 23 500 = 0.001464 mm.
Convert to micrometres: 0.001464 mm x 1000 = 1.46 um (3 s.f.).

questions.question: Which describes how ATP is synthesised by chemiosmosis? A H+ pumped from the matrix to the intermembrane space, B H+ diffuse from the intermembrane space to the matrix through ATP synthase, C H+ diffuse from the intermembrane space to the stroma through ATP synthase, D H+ jump from inner to outer membrane (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - hydrogen ions diffuse from the intermembrane space to the matrix through ATP synthase.
steps: Electron transport pumps H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a gradient.
H+ then diffuse back down the gradient through ATP synthase in the inner membrane.
The energy released drives ADP + Pi to ATP in the matrix.
Option C mentions the stroma (chloroplasts) and option D is not a process of mitochondria, so B is correct.

questions.question: Amytal inhibits the electron transport chain in respiration. Which row of the table shows the changes caused by amytal in a cell? (1 mark)
questions.answer: B: oxygen used decreases and Krebs cycle activity decreases
steps: Amytal blocks the electron transport chain, so oxygen is not used as the final electron acceptor and oxygen use falls.
Reduced NAD and FAD are then not re-oxidised, so the Krebs cycle (which needs oxidised NAD) slows down as well.

questions.question: Which molecule is required in the conversion of pyruvate to a 2-carbon compound in the link reaction? A oxidised NAD, B oxidised NADP, C reduced NAD, D reduced NADP (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - oxidised NAD.
steps: In the link reaction pyruvate is decarboxylated and oxidised to acetyl CoA.
Oxidation removes hydrogen, which is accepted by NAD+ (oxidised NAD) to form reduced NAD.
So oxidised NAD is needed as the hydrogen acceptor.
Reduced NAD and NADP are products or the wrong form, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Name three products of the Krebs cycle (2 marks).
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide, reduced NAD and reduced FAD (ATP or GTP is also produced).
steps: The Krebs cycle decarboxylates the acetyl group, releasing carbon dioxide.
Hydrogen is transferred to NAD+ and FAD, producing reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
A small amount of ATP (or GTP) is made by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Any three of these products give the answer.

questions.question: Comment on the conclusions that can be made from the graphs of mitochondrial number and ATP quantity after cell division and during differentiation of brain cells (4 marks).
questions.answer: Both mitochondrial number and ATP concentration rise during differentiation, supporting the idea that more mitochondria make more ATP, but ATP rises far less than the mitochondrial number.
steps: The number of mitochondria per neurone rises from about 15 on day 1 to about 90 on day 5 and 545 on day 10, with a sharp rise after day 5, about 36-fold overall.

ATP concentration rises from about 3.2 to 7.5 a.u., only about 2.3 times, with a plateau between days 5 and 7, so it is not directly proportional (much of the ATP is being used for growing axons and forming synapses).

The error bars for ATP overlap on days 1 and 3 and on days 5 and 7 so some increases may not be significant, but the rise to day 10 is clear and the mitochondria error bars do not overlap after day 5.
The correlation does not prove that mitochondria cause the rise in ATP, and results come only up to 10 days.

questions.question: Which label on the brain cross-section identifies the pituitary gland? A J, B K, C L, D M (1 mark).
questions.answer: A: J
steps: J points to the small dark gland attached to the underside of the brain, in the hollow of the skull above the nasal cavity, which is the pituitary gland.
K is the cerebral hemisphere, L the brain stem (hypothalamus/medulla region) and M the cerebellum.

questions.question: Explain how growth hormone (a peptide hormone) stimulates the synthesis of protein in muscle (3 marks).
questions.answer: GH binds receptors on muscle cells, activating a signalling pathway that increases transcription of genes for proteins and the production of IGF-1, so protein synthesis increases.
steps: GH is a peptide hormone, so it cannot cross the membrane and binds to receptors on the muscle cell surface.
Binding activates a signal transduction pathway inside the cell (such as JAK/STAT).
The pathway increases transcription of genes for muscle proteins and for IGF-1, which stimulates further growth.
Increased mRNA is translated on ribosomes, so more muscle protein is synthesised.

questions.question: Comment on the changes in the concentration of growth hormone in the blood of males of different ages, using the graph (3 marks).
questions.answer: GH concentration in males falls sharply from childhood to about age 30, then falls slowly and levels off at about 5 to 8 ng dm^-3 after about 40.
steps: It falls from about 50 ng dm^-3 at age 10 to about 23 at 18 and about 12 at 28, a fall of about 75 % by age 30, the steepest part of the curve.
After about 40 years it changes little (about 6 to 8 ng dm^-3 up to 73 and about 5 at 86), so it is lower in older people than in young ones.
The error bars are large and overlap for many of the older ages (e.g. 28, 34 and 73), so small differences between these ages may not be significant.

questions.question: Which hormone is the fight or flight hormone? A adrenaline, B amylopectin, C cholesterol, D statin (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - adrenaline.
steps: Adrenaline is the hormone released by the adrenal medulla during fight or flight.
Amylopectin is a component of starch, not a hormone.
Cholesterol is a lipid precursor of steroid hormones, and statins are cholesterol-lowering drugs.
So the answer is A, adrenaline.

questions.question: Describe how mouse cells can be genetically modified to synthesise human growth hormone (4 marks).
questions.answer: Isolate the human GH gene, insert it into a vector with a promoter, transfer the vector into mouse cells, select cells that took it up, and culture them so they express and secrete GH.
steps: Isolate the human GH gene (for example from mRNA by reverse transcription to make cDNA).
Insert the gene into a vector such as a plasmid, using restriction enzymes and ligase, with a suitable promoter.
Transfer the vector into the mouse cells, for example by transfection or electroporation.
Select and culture the modified cells, which express the human GH gene and secrete the hormone into the medium.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using genetically modified mouse cells rather than E. coli to produce human GH (2 marks).
questions.answer: Advantage: mammalian cells carry out post-translational modification so GH folds correctly; disadvantage: culturing mammalian cells is slower and more expensive than growing E. coli.
steps: Mouse cells are eukaryotic, so they can fold, glycosylate and modify the protein as human cells do.
E. coli cannot always carry out these modifications, so its protein may be inactive.
Mouse cell culture is slower, needs more expensive growth media and has lower yields than E. coli.
So one advantage and one disadvantage are given.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of a motor neurone by naming the parts labelled A to C (2 marks).
questions.answer: A: dendrite; B: cell body; C: myelin sheath (Schwann cell)
steps: A points to a thin branching process that carries impulses towards the cell body: a dendrite.
B points to the main body of the neurone containing the nucleus: the cell body.
C points to one of the sausage-shaped insulating segments along the axon: a myelin sheath formed by a Schwann cell.

questions.question: Describe how a nerve impulse is conducted across the synapse between neurones (3 marks).
questions.answer: The impulse causes Ca2+ entry, vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, and it diffuses to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na+ channels to generate a new impulse.
steps: The action potential reaches the presynaptic knob and Ca2+ channels open.
Ca2+ enters and causes vesicles to release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
This opens Na+ channels, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane and generating a new action potential.

questions.question: Explain why L-DOPA, given orally in tablet form, reduces the symptoms of Parkinson's disease (4 marks).
questions.answer: L-DOPA is absorbed from the gut into the blood, crosses the blood-brain barrier, is converted to dopamine in the brain, and restores dopamine signalling.
steps: Taken orally, L-DOPA is absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
Dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, but L-DOPA can.
Once in the brain, L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by the enzyme decarboxylase.
The extra dopamine restores transmission at synapses in the motor pathways, reducing symptoms.

questions.question: Which is a function of the medulla oblongata? A control of the cardiac response, B long-term memory, C release of ADH, D voluntary movement (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - control of the cardiac response.
steps: The medulla oblongata is in the brainstem and controls involuntary functions such as heart rate and breathing.
It contains the cardiac control centre, which changes heart rate via the autonomic nervous system.
Long-term memory is a function of the cerebrum, and voluntary movement is controlled by the motor cortex.
ADH is released by the posterior pituitary, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Discuss the role of bacteria, inflammation and lifestyle in ageing, using the graphs of the changes in bacteria and inflammation during healthy and unhealthy ageing (6 marks).
questions.answer: Ageing brings more harmful bacteria, fewer protective ones and more inflammation, which rise faster with an unhealthy lifestyle; a healthy lifestyle slows these changes and keeps people healthy for longer.
steps: Graph 1: pathogenic bacteria increase with age, and the rise is steeper in unhealthy ageing, reaching a higher level over a shorter life.
Graph 2: protective bacteria decrease with age, and fall faster in unhealthy ageing, so the pathogenic bacteria are no longer controlled.

Graph 3: inflammation increases with age and more steeply in unhealthy ageing, so more pathogens and fewer protective bacteria go with more inflammation, which can damage tissues in different parts of the body (e.g. gut, joints and blood vessels) and add to age-related disease.

Lifestyle factors such as a poor diet, lack of exercise, smoking and stress would favour pathogens and inflammation, whereas a healthy diet and exercise help keep protective bacteria and reduce inflammation.
The graphs show the trends only (no values), and association does not prove that bacteria cause the inflammation.

questions.question: Which molecule detects light during germination of seeds? A chlorophyll, B phytochrome, C retinal, D rhodopsin (1 mark).
questions.answer: B - phytochrome.
steps: Phytochrome is the photoreceptor in plants that detects red and far-red light.
It controls germination and other light-dependent responses in seeds.
Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis, not for detecting germination signals.
Retinal and rhodopsin are animal photoreceptor molecules, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Determine the effect of light (red, blue and white light at low and high intensities) on the growth of peanut seedlings, using the graphs (4 marks).
questions.answer: Red light gives the tallest seedlings, then blue, then white, at both intensities, and plants grow much more in high light intensity, while those in low intensity die after 32 days.
steps: High intensity: seedlings grow steadily for 55 days, with red light the best (about 19 to 42 cm), blue about 10 to 24 cm and white only about 7 to 15 cm.
Low intensity: there is little growth (red about 16 to 17, blue about 12 to 14 and white about 6 to 9 cm) and the plants died after 32 days.

So the colour matters: red light (acting through phytochrome) promotes elongation more than blue or white light, which contains blue, so the seedlings are less tall, and a higher intensity gives more height for the same colour (red 28 cm against 17 cm at 32 days).
Each point appears to be a single value, so the differences have no statistical test.

questions.question: Explain how auxin causes cells to increase in size, given that auxin stimulates the release of H+ ions that disrupt cellulose microfibrils and the uptake of K+ ions (4 marks).
questions.answer: Auxin activates proton pumps, so H+ is released into the cell wall, loosening cellulose and allowing expansion; K+ uptake lowers water potential, so water enters and the cell enlarges.
steps: Auxin stimulates proton pumps in the cell surface membrane, which move H+ into the cell wall.
The lower pH activates enzymes (expansins) that break bonds between cellulose microfibrils, loosening the wall.
Auxin also stimulates uptake of K+ into the cell, lowering the water potential inside.
Water enters by osmosis, the vacuole and cell enlarge, and the wall stretches as the cell increases in size.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage change in germination between 200 ppm and 400 ppm gibberellin, as a whole number, using the table of results (2 marks).
questions.answer: 60 % decrease
steps: Number germinating at 200 ppm = 114 and at 400 ppm = 46, so the change is 46 - 114 = -68.
Percentage change = -68 / 114 x 100 = -59.6 %, which is a decrease of 60 % to a whole number.

questions.question: Explain how gibberellins affect germination of the ashoka tree seeds in this investigation (2 marks).
questions.answer: Gibberellin switches on genes for amylase, which hydrolyses stored starch to sugars that the embryo uses for respiration and growth, so germination is promoted.
steps: Gibberellin is released in the embryo and binds to receptors in the aleurone cells.
This switches on genes for amylase, which is produced and secreted.
Amylase hydrolyses starch in the endosperm to maltose and glucose, supplying the embryo with energy.
The energy supports respiration and growth of the embryo, so the seed germinates.

questions.question: Which describes the effect lidocaine has on the membranes of neurones? A it closes sodium ion channels, B increases the number of action potentials, C it opens potassium ion channels, D it opens sodium ion channels (1 mark).
questions.answer: A - it closes sodium ion channels.
steps: Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, so they cannot open.
Without Na+ entry, depolarisation and action potentials are prevented.
Lidocaine does not increase action potentials or open potassium channels, so B and C are wrong.
Opening Na+ channels would cause the opposite effect to lidocaine, so D is wrong.

questions.question: Which describes the effect of MDMA (ecstasy) on neurones? A damages the myelin sheath, B decreases release of neurotransmitters, C decreases the speed of action potentials, D increases release of neurotransmitters (1 mark).
questions.answer: D - it increases the release of neurotransmitters.
steps: MDMA causes neurones to release more serotonin and dopamine, increasing neurotransmitter release.
This increases the effect of the neurotransmitters at synapses.
It is not known to damage myelin directly, and it does not slow action potentials, so A and C are wrong.
Decreasing release (B) is the opposite of what MDMA does, so D is the answer.

questions.question: Suggest how TTX, which binds to ion channels in neurones, could inhibit the nervous control of breathing (3 marks).
questions.answer: TTX blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in neurones of the medulla and phrenic/intercostal nerves, so action potentials cannot be generated and the diaphragm and intercostal muscles are not stimulated to breathe.
steps: TTX binds to voltage-gated sodium channels in the membranes of neurones.
Na+ cannot enter, so depolarisation and action potentials are not produced.
Neurones of the medulla that control breathing cannot send impulses to the respiratory muscles.
The diaphragm and intercostal muscles are not stimulated, so breathing is reduced or stops.

questions.question: Give the meaning of LD50 = 8.4 g per kg, using the information in the graph (1 mark).
questions.answer: The dose of TTX that kills 50% of the mice tested is 8.4 g per kg body mass.
steps: LD50 is the lethal dose at which 50% of the test population die.
On the graph, the percentage dying reaches 50% at a dose of 8.4 g per kg.
So 8.4 g per kg of TTX is the dose that kills half of the mice.
This is a measure of the toxicity of the substance.

questions.question: Comment on the toxicity of TTX in mice, using the graph of percentage of mice dying at each dose (3 marks).
questions.answer: TTX is highly toxic: very small doses kill mice, with none dying up to 6.0 ug kg^-1 but all dying at 10 ug kg^-1, so the lethal dose lies in a narrow range.
steps: No mice died at 6.0 ug kg^-1 or less, then the percentage dying rises steeply (about 4 % at 6.5, 22 % at 7.5, 50 % at about 8.5 and 90 % at 9.5), so it is dose-dependent.
All the mice died at 10.0 ug kg^-1, only 4 ug kg^-1 above the highest dose with no deaths, so a small increase in dose changes the outcome a lot.
The LD50 of 8.4 ug kg^-1 is very small (about 0.0084 mg per kg), so TTX is toxic even in tiny amounts; the points are close to the line of best fit, so it fits well.
